maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: Consideration of the motion of Mr. Kelly for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Sutherland resumed from Monday, March. 10.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with those other speakers who congratulated the mover (Mr. Kelly) and the seconder (Mr. Lapierre)-of the Address. I particularly feel pleased to congratulate the hon. gentleman who comes from the same section of the country as I do, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) on the honour that has been conferred upon him asking him to second the Address. At the same time, I must confess that he is not here through any fault of mine. May I add, that I join in the sympathy that has been expressed to those ministers and
The Address-Mr. Manion

others who are sick and absent from the House at this time.
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the Address is usually made up of speeches dealing with the subjects brought up in the Speech from the Throne itself. As very many subjects are touched upon, one is not at a loss to deal with any one subject; but after having read the Speech of His Excellency a number of times I have come to the conclusion, that it is made up of four main types of clauses: First, clauses of double meaning and intent; second, pious hopes for the future; third, promises of better conduct; and, fourth misstatements of fact. I do not intend to make this statement without offering some proof of what I say.
In regard to clauses of double meaning and intent, one has only to read the clause regarding the St. Lawrence waterway. I notice in the papers that those who are opposed to that scheme view that clause as an encouragement to them, while those who are supporting the scheme have taken it las of some encouragement to themselves.
As to pious hopes for the future, these appear in the references to stabilization of freight rates and the cost of living. This cost of living question, like King Charles' head in writings of poor Mr. Dick, pops up every now and then.
The government's promises of better conduct deal with estimates and expenditures, and the misstatements of fact deal with past economies and the prosperity of the country. In regard to past economies, I think most members of this House would have to delve pretty deeply to find them. One case I might mention, and that is the appointment of a new Auditor General at a salary of $15,000, a position for which a salary of $6,000 was considered quite sufficient in the past. I have nothing whatever to say regarding the gentleman who was appointed, because I presume he is a most estimable gentleman, but in the past $6,000 was considered ample salary for the position, and I think one would have to reverse the telescope to find how that innovation was helping in the direction of economy.
In regard to prosperity, the Prime Minister has put into the mouth of His Excellency in the Speech, and mentioned again in his own address, as have some other members who have spoken, that marked prosperity exists in Canada to-day. Well, Sir, I am unable to discover it. I have been in many towns and cities in Canada, and I have heard the discussions here in which members from the farming sections in this country have 
participated, and I have yet to discover where there is real prosperity in the Dominion of Canada at the present time. In fact, I think that what we have at the present time is mainly dissatisfaction, discontent, and unrest.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, that comes from the
dissatisfaction that exists. Sir, I should like to ask, what is the matter with Canada that these conditions should exist? Here we have a magnificent country, a country with all the attributes of a great nation, a country with a population so small that it is practically no population at all compared with the area of the country. When you compare the magnificent area of this country with that of the United States, where they have 110,000,000 people and room for as many more, while we have only 9,000,000, and compare it with Europe where, leaving out Russia, they have some 300,000,000 of people while we have only 9,000,000 in double the area, one wonders rvhy this condition should exist in Canada. Then, when you take into consideration our vast resources-our minerals, our fisheries, our timber and pulp and lumber interests, our millions of acres of fertile land, and all the other resources which we have-one might well ask himself, why should these conditions be as they are at the present time? It is true that the Prime Minister offered an explanation of these conditions. According to my recollection he mentioned that one of the causes was the fact that we had appointed a great many civil servants, and another of the causes had something to do with the Intercolonial railway. May I say here, Sir, that I do not like discussing the Prime Minister's speech in his absence, although I am going to do it. I do not like to do it when he is not here, but it is not my fault that is is strolling up and down the Boardwalk at Atlantic city instead of leading the House. Furthermore, he will have the opportunity finally to reply if he chooses to do so, because he can speak again on the amendment which has been offered.
I wish to indicate what I think are the real causes of the dissatisfaction and discontent in Canada at this time. To my mind there are three main ones: First, high taxes; second, the broken promises of the Prime Minister himself; third, the destructive tariff legislation which is strangling the industrial life of our country, which is indeed strangling our country as a whole. Sir, I shall endeavour to elaborate those three causes and that shall be the total of my speech, al-

The Address-Mr. Manion
though that elaboration may occupy some little time.
The fact of the high taxes requires no elaboration. Everybody in this country knows that we are suffering from a tremendous burden of taxation. The very fact that this government has realized at last that we are suffering from taxation is proof enough that everybody else in the country knows it. Economy, Sir, is imperative in this country. Everybody admits that, and I am very pleased that in the Speech from the Throne there is some promise of economy. That is sufficient for the elaboration of that subject; it needs no further amplification from me.
In regard to the broken promises of the Prime Minister, that is a subject I shall deal with at a little more length. I think in that regard the Prime Minister has made a record. When you compare him with any other public man we have ever had in Canada he certainly has made a record, in breaking promises if he has not in making them. It seems to me, Sir, that in the case of broken promises his appetite grew with its indulgence. And then at times, when he did not find promises were sufficient, he appointed commissions. He has already appointed I do not know how many commissions. I made an attempt to-day to find out how many commissions have been appointed by this government in the two years in which they have been in power. One prominent gentleman in this House guessed there were a dozen or more. I have been endeavouring to ascertain the number myself, and I shall just mention three or four which come to my recollection. There was a commission on questions affecting the returned soldiers; a commission on the rates charged by steamships; a commission on pulpwood; and a commission on grain. Those are four prominent commissions, four -large and expensive commissions. The pulp-wood commission is still sitting, and the grain commission is still sitting; and I am informed by an authority high up in the Department of Trade and Commerce that the grain commission is costing this country to-day-and it has been sitting for a long time-something like $800 per diem. But, not satisfied with appointing so many commissions in the past, I notice that in the Speech from the Throne we are promised two more.
I remember, and you will remember, Mr. Speaker, you who are a student of French history, that just before the French Revolution, when the people were crying for bread, I think it was Marie Antoinette said " Give
them cake." In Canada when the people are crying out from the distressing conditions which prevail the Prime Minister says "Let us give them another commission." It is true that revolutions have not been popular in Canada, but I venture to make this prophecy -that when the opportunity next comes to the electors they will bring about such a political revolution as will put my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and his associates in the wilderness from whence they came in 1921.
Now, Sir, just to specify three or four broken promises of the Prime Minister,-because I do not wish to make statements which I cannot prove: In the first place, the Prime Minister promised to the soldiers of this country that they would get better treatment than we were giving them. He travelled from Halifax to Vancouver, and he promised them that they would get very much better treatment. He implied that we were treating the soldiers badly, and he promised that if he was given power he would grant them relief. Instead of that-so far as I can find out, and I say this in all sincerity-since this government has come into power the soldiers have found that the strings have been tightened very much more than when we were in power in every possible way, and to my mind it has been more difficult for the soldiers to get the justice which is coming to them. From end to end of Canada, on that ground, there is a dissatisfied feeling amongst the soldiers of this country.
Then there was the second promise which I mentioned, that in regard to the cost of living. That was a favourite cry with the Prime Minister. He played many a tune upon that instrument. He blamed us for the high cost of living. Instead of the cost of living going down since the Prime Minister came into power it has gone up. In fact, living is so difficult to obtain for the working men of Canada that they are emigrating at the rate of fifteen or twenty thousand a month. I got the following figures from the Bureau of Statistics of the Department of Trade and Commerce, the index price figures for a series of years. The index figure for wholesale prices for 1913 they put at par, which was 100. In 1920, when there was a general boom throughout the world, the figure reached its very highest which was 243. In 1921 while our government was still in power the index figure dropped 72 points to 171. This government came into power in December, 1921. In 1922 -too soon for any effect from their actions, if any blame is to be attributable to them for an increase in the cost of living, or if they
The Address-Mr. Manion

are to be given any credit for relief-the figure dropped to 152 from 171, a drop of 19 points. But in the last year, that is in 1923, the first year for which they can really be given credit or discredit if they are to be held responsible for the condition of affairs, the figure again rose to 153. So that the cost of living has not been reduced to the working people as was promised to them.
There was another favourite cry of the Prime Minister, and he was greatly assisted in that by our genial friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock), in regard to doing away with combines, trusts and mergers. I can almost hear the Minister of Labour still striking that note, which he struck so often during the campaign, on "combines, trusts and mergers." The people were told that we were linked up with them. Hon. gentlemen opposite said they were going to show the people what they would do with combines trusts and mergers when they got into power. Well, they got into power, and it is true that last year they brought in legislation to deal with the matter, but that legislation is now pigeon-holed, so far as I can understand, and it will be a long time before it will be withdrawn from its hiding place.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You need not think it is pigeon-holed.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If it is not pigeon-holed
the minister has done nothing with it so far as I can discover.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is functioning perfectly.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Perhaps it has not been
pigeon-holed, it has been dropped in the waste-paper basket. The Prime Minister in his speech the other day brought up the question of these combines, trusts and mergers, and criticized us foj not having taxed "the profiteers." We were blamed for not having sufficiently taxed the men who had made fortunes during the war although they still had those fortunes when hon. gentlemen themselves came into power.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They were all Tories.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
All the more reason why
the Prime Minister should have gone after them if he was sincere in his proposition. I am quite sure if he were convinced they were all Tories he would have done so.
Finally there was one other favourite promise, and that is all I shall mention of the broken promises of the Prime Minister. That is in regard to responsible government. That was a particular hobby of the right hon. gen-
tleman. I can remember well sitting in this House in 1920 and 1921 and listening to his speeches in which he abused us, like so many thugs, for being usurpers of power, for doing away with responsible government in this country, for violating the fundamental principles of democracy, for practising a colossal crime upon the people of Canada when we did not have a proper mandate from the people. I remember well those speeches.	And yet at that time
we had a majority I think of thirty in the House of Commons over all the existing parties. And to-day the Prime Minister is in a minority of two or three.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Four.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He is in a minority of four. Under these circumstances, since he is such an apostle of responsible government, I should think it would be his duty to carry on during the session, bring down all necessary legislation, and as soon as possible go to the country and get a proper mandate from the people or let someone else get it. But, instead of doing that, he simply goes on promising new legislation of whatever kind he thinks will bring votes. The other day he leaned across to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), leader of the Progressives and told him if only he would give him his support, he would bring down legislation which would be satisfactory to him. He first attempted apparently to persuade the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). Not having succeeded in doing that he approached, as a last resort, the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) at the present time. And a rather amusing thing it was to me, after the Speech from the Throne had been delivered, and almost before the ink was dry upon the paper, the hon. member for Brandon hurried forward, almost with indecent haste, to assure the Prime Minister that he need not fear any. embarrassment from him. I do not know that there was any need of such assurance, there certainly was not in this section of the House.
These are some of the promises which have been broken by the Prime Minister. I might go on for some hours if I wished, mentioning other broken promises, but these were outstanding instances. There was a veritable flood of promises, but a veritable damming back of their fulfilment. It was a case of running away from them and dodging them, ever since the Liberal platform of the Liberal party was framed in 1919. It was a veritable retreat from Moscow, a rout; but the Prime

The Address-Mr. Manion
Minister should remember that after the retreat from Moscow came Waterloo; and he should also ponder over the fact that that other great political general who made promises which he did not carry out, Mr. Drury, is spending his time on his farm.
I think you, Mr. Speaker, who have read British literature, will remember Dicken's famous character, Mr. Micawber. He was a delightful ne'er-do-well, always in debt; and when pressed by a creditor he would give a promissory note which he never intended to pay, and then would sit back complacently in his chair and say, "Well, thank God, that debt is paid". The Prime Minister reminds me very much of Micawber. When he is pressed by the Progressive party he gives them another promise, and as they hasten forward to accept it with an innocence that Bret Harte would describe as childlike and bland, he sits back with Micawber-like complacency, and says, "Thank God that account is settled". I venture to make the assertion that Micawber paid as many of his notes as the Prime Minister will ever fulfil of his promises. Sir, because of this continual changing and veering around the policy of the present government might well be described as an advancing, retreating, sidestepping, wabbling vacillating, vote-hunting policy. There has been a change with every breath of popular feeling so much so that their policy reminds me of a southern politician, a great statesman, who at one time made a speech to his constituency and concluded in this way; " Gentlemen, them is my principles, but if they don't suit you I can change them." Is it any wonder that we have from one end of Canada to the other, discontent, dissatisfaction and unrest? I do not think so.
Now, I intend dealing with the third cause of unrest, which is the destructive tariff policy which is strangling our industrial life, and indeed strangling our country as a whole. In the Liberal platform of 1919 free trade was practically promised to the people of the country. However, as that was put forward for the purpose of getting the farmer vote, and did not succeed, it was one of the broken promises which I did not mention before. After the Liberal party came into power it is true the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding), in 1922, did make a few reductions in the tariff, and also promised my hon. friends to my left that this was only a beginning. I remember his words. Then in 1923, a year later, he came forward with a few more reductions. But, Sir, he was struck with the fact that he was performing a dangerous feat,
and he made a speech regarding this question.
I am going to quote his (Mr. Fielding's) words, because they are worth quoting at this time. He said that stability of the tariff was needed if we were ever to get satisfactory results and were to have prosperity in the country. On May 11, 1923, just ten months ago to-day, Mr. Fielding said-
There is a thought which does not receive as much consideration as I think sometimes it should be given in public discussions, and that is the desirability of something like tariff stability. It is desirable that something like an assurance of tariff stability should be given to business men. Exceptions will occur. There will be cases where, in the interest of the consumer, reductions in the tariff ought to be made. But the conditions to which I refer are exceptional. Speaking broadly, it is possible to give the country a reasonable assurance of stability of tariff. Such assurances are very desirable, for no business man would care to enter upon enterprises which may be brought into peril by frequent tariff changes. The tariff as it will be when the changes proposed to-day come into effect will be-a moderate tariff and probably as low as the country can afford to have under present conditions.
Later in his address he said:
Subject to the exceptional conditions such as I have mentioned I think the country should be content to accept the tariff as it will now stand as one as fair and reasonable as can be prepared under all the circumstances, and business men should be able to carry on the various enterprises without the fear of being soon disturbed by further changes.
Those are the remarks, Sir, of the Finance Minister of that day, and by the way he is still Finance Minister of Canada, but despite that fact, and despite the fact that he is sick in bed, the present government comes forward with a Speech from the Throne which is a betrayal of the Finance Minister-not only a betrayal of that minister, but a betrayal of the industrial interests of this country, because a sigh of relief went up from the industrial concerns -when they were promised some measure of stability.

I remember well at one time Lincoln was asked if he had not taken a different stand1 at that time than he took the year previously. He said "Yes, I have taken a different stand to-day from that which I took last year, and any man who is not wiser to-day than he was yesterday is not much of a man."

speechtext:
The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) might agree with me that when a man changes his opinion he should acknowledge it, but when the Prime Minister changes his opinion he stands up and tells us he is in the same position as he was last year.
And, Sir, if I may continue, this betrayal of the industrial interests of the country is being carried on in spite of the depression which exists, in spite of the exodus from this country, of fifteen or twenty thousand per month of our finest young men. To hold the knife of the free trade guillotine above the necks of the industrial leaders of this country cannot lead to anything but dissatisfaction and unrest, and it is leading to that condition.
I shall now name five different industries that have been affected. The woollen industry has been seriously affected. A number of the woollen plants are idle. The Perth woollen mill, which ran along for forty-five years from the introduction of the National Policy in 1878 till this year, is now closed down for the first time. Then the boot and shoe industry is suffering from the same condition. They are suffering from the increase in the British preference, from the depreciated exchange of Britain, and from the fact that the price of labour is about half the price in Britain than it is in Canada. So that they are practically being pushed out of business.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Prime Minister said the other day that they would not be affected.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, he did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Very slightly. I am not Prime Minister. The hon. gentleman seems to be a prophet at short distance.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The increase in the British preference affected them; at any rate, they are being affected just as the other industries in the country are being affected. Then we have the farm implement industry in such a

position that it is going to be ruined. I hold in my hand a statement from one of the financial papers regarding the Massey-Harris Company, which is one of the largest farm implement manufacturing companies in Canada, and it shows, Sir, that they sustained a net loss last year of $22,448, and now this industry is going to be wiped out altogether. Coming a little nearer home, there are two industries in my own city which are vitally affected-the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) would be easily able to identify them-by the present cuts in the tariff. One of them-I do not intend to name either of them, because I have not their permission to do so-was an industry which in my city was employing some 300 men; and has a plant in eastern Ontario employing about the same number. Both these plants, and perhaps others for all I know, are closed at the present time. I have it from the leaders in that industry that by a very slight change in the tariff, or a very slight change in the sales tax, they could go on as they did for very many years in my city and in that eastern town, and supply the prairie provinces with their product. Then, I was on the train the other evening and I met an old friend of mine from the home city of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. He is the travelling head of one of our big corporations. As he has a plant in Fort William I asked him how business was, and he described how they were running at present on half time. He pointed out that they were being driven out of business not by British or by United States competition, but by French competition, because the French franc is down to about three or four cents; French labour is probably even cheaper than the British; and the duty on the product is so low that it allows the French product to come in and beat them. I have a great respect for the French people, indeed I have a love for them; but I have much greater love for the Canadian people, and I do not believe it is fair that our Canadian industries should be driven out in favour of French industries. That same company wrote me as I communicated with them asking for details. I have under my hand their letter in reply, in which they point out that while in Canada, they cannot compete with the French industries, they are running at a loss of about four dollars a ton on their product, operating on half time, and continuing in business for the sole purpose of holding their organization together in the hope that perhaps this government will come to its senses and give them some relief. This same product is now being

The Address-Mr. Manion
manufactured and sold in the United States at a price on the basis of which this company could sell and make money; and that is because in the United States they have sense enough to protect their own industries. So here are five industries which illustrate my point-many others could be mentioned, but I think I have dealt with enough to serve the purpose.
The fact remains that no industry in Canada to-day is safe. No industrial leader knows when he is going to be slaughtered and thrown to the wolves to keep this government in power.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is a long
way from power, though.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Not nearly so long as the hon. gentleman is. Sir, would any sane man invest his money in an industrial plant in Canada under these circumstances? Would any sane man who has control of foreign capital think of bringing it into Canada and investing it? The answer is so obvious that it is not necessary to state it.
Canada alone of all countries is talking of adopting free trade. Do my hon. friends from the prairie provinces believe that all the wisdom of the ages has been extracted and passed out to that part of the country? Do they think that other nations with the exception, we will say, of Great Britain-and I will touch upon that in a moment-have no wisdom; that this little country of nine million people should think of lowering tariffs while all others deem it necessary to have protection? Why, Sir, even England made veiy great progress under protection. England did not have free trade until 1846, and when they adopted free trade as their policy it was after they had built up an immense line of manufacturing plants and an immense capitalistic system which enabled them to compete with and oust practically any manufacturing country in the world. Then, and not till then, did England think of adopting a free trade policy. When she felt that she could hold her own market because she could undersell any other country and because other countries had not achieved the stage of development that she had, then she proposed free trade. Cofoden, himself a manufacturer, prophesied that within ten years every country in the world would adopt free trade. If every country had done that it is altogether likely that England would have profited by her free trade. As it is, she had received such a momentum under protection, she had built up such an organization under protection, that until a few years ago she was profiting very highly by her free trade system,
underselling as she was, many other countries. The very act which she brought into force at that time and under which raw materials and foodstuffs were admitted into England cheaply, so cheaply that she could get them at as low prices as any other country in the world could, was in a sense the very best protection she could give to her manufacturing industries which were then so highly established. That, then, was the attitude of England. Now even England has adopted some of the protectionist system that we have in her key industries act. It is true that in a recent election she defeated protection, but I venture to assert that if Mr. Baldwin had taken three months instead of three weeks to educate the people of England away from the free trade policy which has prevailed in that country for eighty years, he would have succeeded, to England's very great benefit.
As it is-I mention this because the case of England is so often flaunted in our faces- what are the conditions in that free trade country? I do not know any country where the conditions are worse at the moment. There are about two million unemployed, and that means eight million who have nothing with which to buy their food. The people are emigrating from England even faster than they are emigrating from Canada. The case of England appears to be one which it is well worth pointing out to my hon. friends to my left. Some of them take the attitude-I do not attribute it to all of them-that the only wealth produced in Canada is that produced on the prairie farms. Well I submit that the man who takes the raw leather and turns it into boots and shoes is just as much a creator of wealth as the man who raises the animals from which the leather was taken. I submit, further, that the man who takes the wool and turns it into woollen goods, also the one who carries the operation further and turns the woollen goods into clothing, is just as much a creator of wealth as the man who raises the sheep. Furthermore, the manufacturer who takes the wheat and turns it into flour is just as truly a creator of wealth as the man who grew the wheat from which the flour was made. It is a point worth remembering, because after all we do not wish to destroy any source of wealth in our country.
If you look over the commercial history of the world you will find that all great commercial countries have been built up under protection. I have shown how England did it. At any rate, even if we lay England aside for the moment, the United States, Germany, France-all these countries were built up under a protective tariff. Germany and the
The Address-Mr. Manion

United States were rapidly overtaking England and had indeed surpassed her in many branches before the war.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Does the hon. member not
think that under different circumstances we might be in a happier condition than we are to-day? He appears to be perfectly satisfied with everything, but things do not seem to be so good.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is drawing a conclusion which I do not think he has any right to draw. I am not satisfied with everything; I am trying to offer, as I shall before I have concluded, some ideas the adoption of which would, in my opinion, bring about an improvement of conditions in Canada.. My hon. friend has a right to his opinion just as much as I have to mine, but I say with all due respect that I do not think that his low tariff proposals would improve conditions; I am convinced that they would rather materially hurt conditions in this country.
I was going to say that before the war, German}', which did not really come into the race until about 1870, had under a highly protective system outsold Great Britain and was outselling her in ten of the most important countries in Europe, including Russia. And, by the way, speaking of wealth for a moment again, I should like to refer to one point which I omitted to mention, to show that all wealth is not from agriculture. Various factors besides agriculture go to the production of wealth, and there is no doubt about the fact that England's wealth has not been agricultural; England's wealth has been produced by her manufacturing industries, her trading, and her shipping. England is indeed the least agricultural country of the important nations of the world. Now, Canada resembles the United States in most aspects 

in area, in resources, in climate, and in people-more than she does any other country on the globe. Is it not, then, more sane and logical that we should copy the system of that country in our endeavour to build up the Dominion of Canada than that we should emulate the methods of two little islands on the outskirts of Europe which have an area of about 120,000 square miles, and which together could be placed three times in northern Ontario alone, between' North Bay and the Manitoba boundary?
I agree with the attitude taken last night by the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Kellner); in this regard the hon. gentleman's view is only in keeping with that of Mr. George Langley. My hon. friend from East

Edmonton declared that it is not the tariff that is killing the agricultural industry of the western provinces. Let me quote from the words of George Langley uttered a short time ago. He is a representative farmer and public man, and I do not think that he needs any introduction from me to my western friends. George Langley says:
I do not regard protection as an economic damnation. If we are going to protect our manufacturers, we should protect our farmers, and to help the farmer something definite should be done in respect to transportation.
The hon. member for East Edmonton took exactly that attitude, but I was sorry to see that my hon. friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Kennedy) was of an entirely different opinion.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is East against West.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, the fact is that their views on this question are diametrically opposed. The hon. member for West Edmonton states that if the industries of Canada, after the years of protection that they have had-[DOT] and it may have been only a period of ten years, for that matter-were not able to compete with the rest of the world, it was time that they were allowed to shift for themselves. That is in essence the statement he made. Well, suppose the farmers of the West, after suffering as they did in past years from drought, and after exerting their best efforts for years to make good, found themselves in such a condition that they could not buy seed and were forced to come to whatever government might be in office at the time and ask for assistance, as they have had to do in the past! Suppose, under those circumstances, that government should say to them: "You have been farming long enough now and if you cannot make a success of your business you had better cease operations; you will have to go to the wall."-what would any hon. gentleman say to such an attitude on the part of any government in such a case? Why, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it would be nothing but un-Christian and un-Canadian. By the same token, the attitude of the hon. gentleman from West Edmonton, in regard to the industries of this country, is both unChristian and un-Canadian.
Now I wish to bring to the attention of my hon. friends to my left a point which, I think, is of some interest. What is the promise which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has made that has immediately reached to the heart of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), the leader of the Progressive party? The gist of that promise was that farm implements would be put upon the free

The Address-Mr. Manion
list; at least, that is what anyone would readily infer.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I never said so.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I know my hon. friend die not, but the Prime Minister did.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, the Prime Minister
did not say so in so many words. He is usually in the habit of putting his thoughts in such words that one may draw any conclusion from them that he likes. But in this instance everyone has inferred, from what the Prime Minister has indicated, just what I have stated. Certainly, the inference has not been denied in any part of the country, namely, that farm implements will either be put upon the free list or have a fair reduction made in the duties upon them. Personally, if I were a farmer from the prairie provinces, after my past experience of the Prime Minister, I should be afraid to base any hopes upon any such promise. Nevertheless, as I say, that is the conclusion which everyone draws; and I submit, as was pointed out by my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Hocken) last night, that if that is not the intention of the government it is time that they indicated to the people of the country just what they mean to do; because the makers of farm implements in Canada are in a quandary; they are absolutely in a state of depression, and in fact this business is practically closed up and will remain so until the budget comes down in three or four months' time. Now, what would the cut in farm implements amount to? I made it my business to look into this question and I found that the imports of farm implements into Canada during the last fiscal year amounted to $4,500,000. The duty on that was $680,000. The farming population of Canada is 4,000,000. So that the per capita tax on farm implements last year on the whole of the farming community in the country was seventeen cents. That is what my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has offered as a sop to get the western vote. I must confess it is a rather cheap price if it is intended to purchase votes. I do not say this offensively, but in the Old Testament we are told that Esau sold his birthright for a mess of pottage; it would be a poor mess of pottage that anyone would buy for seventeen cents.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member for
East Edmonton (Mr. Kellner) is not here, and my hon. friend has made a comparison which in my opinion is not quite fair. Does he
not think that it is a little unfair to compare the conditions brought about by nature with conditions over which men. can exercise some control?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I should like to answer my hon. friend's question, but to be candid I do not see his point, and as I am anxious to proceed I shall ask him to pardon me if I do not discuss the question. I was going to point out that the total duties collected last year in the whole of Canada amounted to $133,000,000. That represents $14.50 per head, and if you allotted every farmer of the prairie provinces his share of that, I do not see that it would put the prairies in any more prosperous condition than they are in to-day.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Do all the farmers of
Canada live in the prairie provinces?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, they do not, and I
am glad that, by implication, my hon. friend agrees with me. I shall deal with that aspect in a moment. Let me now come to another point. The prairie farmers have not suffered, by reason of any duties levied1 on farm implements, in the last ten years. For this, I have the word of the leader of the Progressive party who said in his speech that for ten years not a prairie farmer has bought a farm implement at all. Yet, when the Prime Minister offers to take the duties off farm implements, the hon. member immediately jumps into his arms
I am sure that my hon. friends to my left will agree with me, if they will look fairly at the question, that the fact that the conditions in the West are bad has nothing to do, or practically nothing to do, with the tariff. The real reason for present conditions in that part of the country is to be found in world conditions; in the transportation situation; long distances and high rates make it difficult for the farmers to get their products to market. Furthermore, marketing conditions in general would largely affect the situation. These conditions, in my opinion, have very much more to do with the state of affairs in the western provinces to-day than has the tariff.
I remember reading once an opinion of Macaulay's, that if there was one type of taxation which was least productive of benefit to a country, it was robbery I submit that if there is one method by which you can help any industry and which is least productive of benefit to the country, it is the destruction of another industry for the attainment of that purpose. And that is what is proposed in the Speech from the Throne; that is what will, no doubt, be proposed in the budget that
The Address-Mr. Martian

is to be brought down. We are to ruin some sections of the East in order to save the West; and in any case the saving in my opinion is only imaginary.
Now I come to the point raised a moment ago by my hon. friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail); the farmers of Ontario and Quebec must be considered. There are two million people in the prairie provinces. These are not all farmers, but for the sake of argument we will say that they are. But there are more than two million farmers in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and they are all dependent, almost wholly, for the sale of ninety per cent of their products upon the industrial centres of the East. Would it be a fair proposition to ruin these two million farmers of Ontario and Quebec in order to succour the two million of the prairie provinces, even if the sacrifice of the interests of one community would be beneficial to those of the other community?-Which I claim would not be the case.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the Maritime provinces?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I like the Maritime provinces, although from some of the interjections that are being made I wish they had kept some of their representatives at home.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They never change their opinions.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, everybody realizes that the West is in a bad way; no one realizes it better than I do because I am right on the border. But so is all Canada in a bad way. My hon. friend from East York (Mr. Harris) yesterday well described the condition of some manufacturers, friends of his, in Toronto, who had lost in two or three years all that they had made in forty years.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Without whining.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
"Without whining," is
added by some hon. gentleman. But, Sir, all the business men in the towns and cities are suffering from the same depression, and I defy any hon. member to contradict this statement. Therefore while I am ready to do everything I can in a reasonable way-and I am sure all my hon. friends in this section of the House are equally ready-we are not ready to ruin the East to aid the West.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member another question?-perhaps he will be able to see through this one. If the tariff

was increased would not the difference be passed along to the consumer?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is questionable. I do not admit that all the tariff is passed on to the consumer at the present time. Let me ask my hon. friend a question: Suppose a Canadian farmer had a farm just south of Morden, in Manitoba, one-half of which was in the United States, and he raised a thousand bushels of wheat on the Canadian half and another thousand bushels on the American half of his farm. The price of wheat is a little higher in the United States than in Canada; but there is a duty on Canadian wheat going into the United States. Suppose, further, that he wanted to sell his total production in the United States, who would pay the duty on his Canadian wheat, he himself or the consumer on the other side of the line? I submit it would be the fanner.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No. I do not think my question is answered, and I do not think the counter question applies.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I did not expect to satisfy my hon. friend. I was not trying to do so, I was trying to show my own side of the question.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman admit that protection is no advantage to the United States producer in his own country?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not admit anything of that sort. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that protection may not increase prices at all, but it may prevent another country from dumping its surplus products into the protected country, and that is what happens in Canada to-day. Any manufacturer in the United States manufactures on a large scale for 110,000,000 people, but very frequently at the end of the season he has some surplus goods on his hands, and rather than carry the surplus over into the following year he tries to dump it on the Canadian market, and, if he were permitted, he would put out of business the Canadian manufacturer by underselling him, and thereupon proceed to recoup himself out of the pockets of the Canadian people by raising his prices. But, Sir, we do not need to go outside Canada-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is it not true that some of our own manufacturers are doing the same thing with goods that they ship to the British market?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, I have heard it stated that they do.

The Address-Mr. Manion

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why should we protest against dumping if we are doing it ourselves?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am not protesting; but I do object to the foreign manufacturer doing it to us if I can help it. I would not object to my hon. friend hitting back at some man who hit him, but I would object to his hitting at me without reason, and that is what every foreign manufacturer who dumps surplus goods on our markets is doing. I do not blame him, but I do not intend to let him do it if I am awake and can prevent him. The attitude of my hon. friends to my left, in view of the action of the United States government just recently in raising the duty against our wheat, is very peculiar to me. I think it is a most humiliating attitude that we should remain quiescent while the United States impose tariff duties of all kinds against us, a little country of nine million people while they have a population of a hun-
4 p.m. dred and ten million. They are imposing various high duties against the farmers of this country, and the group representing the farmers of the prairie provinces stand here and say:	In return for
the United States hitting us on the right cheek let us turn our left cheek to them for another blow.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman admit that it was the manufacturers of Canada who made it possible for the Canadian farmer to be discriminated against by the United States?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not think the manufacturers of Canada have had anything to do with it. I think the Canadian manufacturer has been the cause of many of our farmers in the past having been in a very prosperous condition. But I was pointing out when I was interrupted that my hon. friends to my left take a most humiliating attitude in turning the other cheek. Two thousand years ago- and I say this not in any spirit of blasphemy -the greatest Christian of us all advocated turning the other cheek, and He was crucified. I have no doubt that my hon. friends will get the same treatment from the American business men at the first opportunity that presents itself to them.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would my hon. friend carry the analogy to its conclusion and say who will be the final victors?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Again I am afraid I do not understand the question.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If any
man to-day advocated remedial measures,
would he not be crucified too, and in less than the thirty-three years that it took the people of His day to crucify the Man of Nazareth?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I hope not, because I am offering remedial measures myself. Knowing my hon. friend as I do, I am quite sure he has no intention of trying to crucify me.
But, Mr. Speaker, the free trade policy was not such a panacea for the economic ills of this country when we had it. Let any hon. member look at the speeches of our public men describing conditions in Canada in 1878, before the national policy was brought into force, and he will find in the debates of that year a statement that when the Prime Minister left the door of the House of Commons conditions were so bad that he was met by a hundred and fifty hungry people who begged him for food or work. That was the state of affairs under practically a free trade policy. Yet the hon. leader of the Farmers' party (Mr. Forke) stated the other night, that we have suffered now for fifty years under protection, and it is time to change the policy. I do not know that it has been all suffering; I think we have had a fairly reasonable amount of progress, and I shall try to prove it. I admit that we have not had the progress that the United States has enjoyed, we have not had the progress that most Canadians would like their country to have had, but we have had a fairly reasonable amount. Let me give a few figures, although I do not like to encumber Hansard with too many statistics. In 1881 we had under acreage less than two and a half million acres; in 1921 our acreage was twenty-three million acres-ten times more than in 1881. The value of our field crops in 1901-I could not get any earlier figures- was $194,000,000; in 1921 it was $931,000,000. The value of our mineral production in 1881 was $10,000,000; in 1921 it had risen to $172,000,000. The total domestic exports were $84,000,000 in 1881, as compared with $1,200,000,000 in 1921. Our wood, paper and wood products were $25,000,000 in 1891, as compared with $284,000,000 in 1921. The life insurance in force was $103,000,000 in 1881, as compared with $3,000,000,000 in the latter year, while the deposits in our banks were $94,000,000 as compared with $2,300,000,000. Now, can any hon. member say that that is not progress? If he has the temerity to do so, then I do not understand what he desires. I repeat, I should like to have seen greater progress, and I am sorry that to-day instead of progressing we are retrogressing. For this lamentable condition I blame the government to a great extent. Sir, when a physician is called in to treat a patient who is in an anaemic, run-down condition, it
The Address-Mr. Manion

is his duty to administer building-up remedies in an endeavour to reconstruct him. But the government, which is the physician of this country at the present time, instead of using building-up remedies for the depressed, rundown condition of the nation is using the antiquated remedy of bleeding. In fact, Sir, it is doing worse, it is trying to save one section of the body politic by amputating another-it is trying to amputate the industrial section of the state.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me a question?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend will allow me to finish, please. What is still worse, it is amputating the legs of the body politic by inches.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend, who was a minister in the late administration, is a medical practitioner, and I understand that the medical world has not yet been able to discover a cure for cancer. Is not the attitude of this government to secure a remedy for the cancer left by the late administration on the country?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I might reply to my hon. friend that if industries are a cancer, that is correct. But I do not consider that industries are a cancer.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend was speaking medically.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Don't put your foot in it again.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The strange thing about the attitude of this government is that they are taking that attitude in spite of the fact that two-thirds of those on the government side- I will not include my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Martell)-are protectionists. In other words, they are placing power before principle; if principle interferes with power so much the worse for the principle, and if the country interferes with power so much the worse for the country. Their attitude, in other words, is, not to relieve the West but to get their votes; and that to my mind means the ruination of this country.
Now, Sir, I am finishing and I intend to say what I consider to be the proper remedy for the conditions that exist. I know it will not appeal to my friends to my left; I do not expect to make many converts, but I believe just as sincerely in this policy as they believe in theirs. I believe that what we need in this country is a reaffirmation of the old National Policy. We need a constructive, protective, national policy for all classes of

the people, a policy which will develop the resources of Canada, a policy which will retain the home market for the Canadian people, a policy which will build up a broader national life and give greater opportunities to the youth of this country, to the sons of farmers as well as to the sons of other people, and here I might just say that no' class of people have done better in the industrial centres than the sons of the farmers, or their forebears, who to-day argue for free trade. We need a policy which will protect us against cheap labour, not only of the Orient but of Europe at the present time. We need a policy that will protect us against dilapidated exchange, because the exchange situation in Europe is in such a shape to-' day that any country can send in its goods over our tariff barrier. We need a policy which will protect us from foreign industry, and by foreign industry I mean any industry outside of Canada, because I am a Canadian first, last and all the time. Are we to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the American and the British people? Not if I can help it, not if my word will have any effect on my people. I believe in keeping Canadian markets for the Canadian people.
Just one word in closing-and I certainly should not mention this if the Prime Minister had not mentioned it-and that is on the question of national unity. That is a favourite theme with the Prime Minister. I do not criticize him for that, but at the same time I do not think it is necessary for anybody in Canada to be continually assuring the people that he desires national unity, I do not know any decent citizen of Canada who does not desire national unity. I may say to my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) that I am sure he would not question my attitude on this question, because I have given him and his confreres a very practical demonstration of the fact that I desire national unity, and as a result my three little boys speak the French language with the same facility that they speak English. Perhaps he would pass that on to the Prime Minister, and may I suggest that the Prime Minister might do a very great service to his country if he would follow my example.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I agree with that part of your speech.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
To my mind the best way to bring about national unity is to bring about national prosperity, and the best way to bring about national prosperity is to bring about a national policy

The Address-Mr. Baldwin
that will build up all sections and develop the resources of the whole country, so that we may build up on the northern half of this continent a great Canadian nation.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
(Stan-stead): Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to use so much of the time of this House that the Upper Chamber, which has been quite lavish in its recommendations, can take any offence. Personally I am not going to follow the see-saw path that has been followed in this House during the last few days, but in my later remarks I shall broaden out and speak more from the national point of view.
I do not think anything has been said in this House that was more popular than when the leader of this government said that he would try to bring the East and the West together, for that is something every true and patriotic Canadian wants. We all want to see the East and West brought together and to have this Canada of ours one great united country.
I would remind the last speaker (Mr. Manion) that he was mistaken in one of his remarks. He made the remark that prior to 1878 there was a free trade party in this country. I wish to tell him that the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie was the Liberal leader in 1878, and he had a duty of 174 per cent ad valorem straight on almost everything. Then the hon. member went on to liken us to the antiquated party. I remember the time of confederation very well. I was quite active in the battle of 1878, and when a man says that there was a free trade party, he really knows better. No one in the province of Quebec has proclaimed since confederation that the Liberal party is a free trade party. The hon. member makes no acknowledgement that he has been corrected.
The very vigorous member for East York (Mr. Harris) last night made a great mistake in speaking of the Grand Trunk Pacific as being in the northern part of the province of Quebec. He must be almost oblivious of his geography, if geography he studied in his boyhood days, to make such a statement, for a glance at the map will show that more than nine-tenths of the province of Quebec lies north of that railway.
I believe that every man who has spoken in this House in the last ten days has had something in his speech that was commendable. I am going to handle the leader of the opposition very gently; I am not going to get into any big fight with him at the present time, but I will just mention one little thing. He went up and down this 15
country until about eight months ago condemning this government, and no bigger charge did he make against it than that they had searched the world and then put Sir Henry Thornton over the National Railways. I do not believe I am making any mistake when I say that he was near the city of Toronto, and perhaps near the Albany Club, when he was told to come off his perch and stop talking about the man who was big enough to handle the great National system of railways. At all events,
I have not noticed in the newspapers that he has made any derogatory remarks about Sir Henry Thornton since then. It is a mighty good thing that people do change their minds sometimes. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) who preceded me talked about a revolution. I do not see any cause for a revolution in this country. There is a process of evolution, and unquestionably things are evolving. An hon. gentleman opposite representing one of the Toronto constituencies gave us an outline of what we might expect to see happen in this old world in the course of a few decades. Things are evolving all around us continually, and a person who cannot see what is happening, not merely in Canada but in the world at large, is wholly lacking in conception.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been hammering away at the leader of the government on wholly fanciful grounds. After the Halifax by-election they made the wires hot with imaginary stories of the alarm he felt at the result. Do we see any manifestation of alarm on the part of the Prime Minister or the members of his government? No, we see nothing of that character. What we do see tends to reassure us. The Prime Minister called Messrs. Dunning and Crerar from the west to consult with them as to the needs of that part of Canada. That was not an evidence of alarm, but. the Tory press-that press which is keeping 'the country ablaze not only by "whispers of death" but by misrepresentation-claimed he was calling these gentlemen down for the purpose of giving them positions in the cabinet. The truth of the matter is he was seeking needed information from them in the public interest.
Dealing with the speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition in the present debate almost every sentence was pungent with sarcasm. I do not propose to answer the right hon. gentlemen, I prefer to deal with the conditions in the country. We have a great and glorious land, such as no other nation on the globe possesses. If we take an inventory of our national resources what do we



The Address-Mr. Baldwin
find? Look at the great province of British Columbia, the second in size in this Dominion. There you find lofty mountains, fertile valleys, and a wealth of timber and minerals. So extensive is that fine province that as my hon. friend the member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) said there was room for empires in some of the valleys in his constituency. We pass eastward and we reach the great province of Alberta with its rich and fertile lands, and the chinook winds which render the climate so mild in winter. We pass on to Saskatchewan and there we find the same rich plains, the same fertile lands, and also enormous deposits of coal and oil. There is no question at all of the wonderful richness of those provinces. Next we reach the province of Manitoba and, like the other prairie provinces, it has been richly endowed by Providence. Next comes the province of Ontario with its enormous wealth. It has gold and silver and nickel mines, and we are told that it even has platinum and radium as well. Its industries are very great and very varied, and the area of its land is immense. Then we come to the greatest of all the provinces, Quebec, with its more than four thousand miles of water line for a border. In that province too there are wonderful natural resources, and like Ontario it possesses mines of great richness and extent. There is no doubt that the mines of Quebec and Ontario, in the course of a decade or two when fully developed, will make our public debt pale into insignificance. I would like to see certain people who get rich, I will not say by what means, and who go to the southern states to squander their money, remain in this country and help to develop the great central provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Surely it would be far better for these people to spend their energy, their money and their time in this land1 of ours which is so "worthy of all the attention we can bestow upon it.
Coming to the Maritime provinces, we find great timber limits, vast areas of minerals, almost inexhaustible fisheries, and fertile fields and valleys. I well recall one beautiful summer evening when I crossed the straits of Northumberland to that beautiful little gem of the sea, Prince Edward Island. I said "This is the most beautiful spot I have yet seen in this Dominion". We arrived at Sum-merside-it was a beautiful evening in the month of August-and as we rode through the country we saw well kept buildings and evidences of prosperity on every hand. My companion said to me "I would like to enter the homes of these people and then I should learn the last word in human happiness and 	' jr I n *|
contentment." I said "You need nc f er these homes. Go to the New England states and there you will find out what the people from these Maritime provinces have accomplished. Or you may go to western Canada as. I have done, and see there people from the Maritime provinces occupying positions of responsibility in every city and every town." I should like to make one recommendation to the people of the Maritime provinces. It is that they should yoke up, marry, have one legislative home. I do not make that suggestion because of their insignificance geographically as compared with the rest of the country. If they lack anything in area they more than make up for it by the brawn and brains of their people. But my story is not yet finished. Think of the great Yukon territory, of the wonderful country in the Mackenzie district, the Franklin district, Baffin's land in the archipelago to the north. If the latter were brought down and attached to Hudson bay, it would make of Canada a huge territory extending north and south for two thousand miles and east and west for three thousand five hundred miles. Is not this wonderful country which I have described such as to make every Canadian proud of the land of his birth or of his adoption?
We may look for great developments in the future through the medium of our waterways. If we glance at the extreme southwestern portion of the province of Ontario wre find that this area is more than one-half water. It seems hard to believe that some day we shall have navigation from the head of the lakes down to the Rainy River district, down the Winnipeg river to lake Winnipeg, and through the Saskatchewan river to the foot hills of the Rockies. This may seem a dream to-day but the future will witness its realization. Let me tell the hon. members of this House that instead of spending so much time fighting we should apply ourselves with all our energy to developing this great country of ours. The waterways we are so fortunate as to possess will ultimately prove the agents of great commercial prosperity in Canada.
We have the greatest inland waterways of the world, from the eastern point of Quebec to the head waters of lake Superior. It is very nearly halfway across the continent, and I am strongly in favour of the deep waterways scheme. This proposition may not be acceptable to a great many hon. members here, but I believe in it thoroughly. I believe that Montreal will ever remain the metropolis of Canada because its great social, financial, religious and industrial advantages will keep it in that position. It is quite within the

The Address-Mr. Baldibin
possibilities of reason that within a very short time a boat drawing thirty feet of water will be able to go from the Atlantic to Montreal, and there is a possibility that Montreal will be a twelve months' port. A certain engineer made a statement in the press that he could dam the straits of Belle Isle and thus provide communication between Newfoundland and the mainland. I remember some eleven years ago in the gulf of St. Lawrence there was a collision with a Norwegian coal boat, and some 1,100 Canadians went down. Now what is thirty million dollars compared with 1,100 lives? It is nothing. If the damming of those straits would warm the gulf, it would improve the temperature of the Maritime provinces, and would put the St. Lawrence in such a condition that boats could run to Montreal the year round. I am somewhat older than many hon. gentlemen in this House and I can remember that when the great Canadian Pacific railway was under construction we were told that the revenue from the road would never pay for the grease used on the axles. But that prediction has proved to be false; so that the man who predicts to-day is considered as a man without discrimination. There are many things we become hazy about.
If we had a twenty-foot channel from Montreal to the head of the lakes it would be very beneficial, because undoubtedly they could not use the lakes more than seven months of the year, while Montreal would be a port for twelve months. There has been great opposition to this scheme, but I think there is no justification for the opposition and that the scheme would be of great benefit. From Calais, Maine, to Florida they oppose the St. Lawrence route. It would be of enormous value to twenty or thirty of the middle or western states-the northwestern states especially. There seems to be a fear that if this waterway were constructed the United States would monopolize it, and that we could not control our own country and its destinies. Why, Mr. Speaker, does anyone believe for one moment that if the United States furnished the capital for the great undertaking it would be any different from any other undertaking at the present time? There are many such undertakings, the Carillon dam proposition, for instance. They have spent some twenty million of dollars on one-on the Grand discharge undertaking. Does anyone think Canada is in danger because an American put up half the money for this enterprise? Does anyone fear that such an undertaking as the deepening of the St. Lawrence river would destroy our country and our unity and injure
15i
our future? I consider it would be a grand advertisement for all Canada and especially Montreal.
I come, Mr. Speaker, from a section of country called the Eastern Townships, twelve or fifteen counties, some 100 miles from the island of Montreal. Someone will ask me, " Why are you interested?" Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that it would be impossible to expend on the island of Montreal, or in that district, hundreds of millions of dollars without creating an immense benefit to the city and the Eastern Townships as well. It would mean the employment of thousands of workmen. The expenditure of money means employment and a benefit to the whole country. If a person is so narrow as to believe that you cannot develop one part of the country without injuring the other, it is a great pity; and such a belief savours too much of parish politics. If we are to have a country like the great nation to the south of us, unquestionably we must develop our resources. The attitude of opposition to this scheme is beyond my comprehension.
In regard to the exodus from Canada, I think no one is more responsible than the late government. In the case of the great republic to the south of us, were they afraid of immigration? No. They received all those who came, and people came from the great centres of Europe, because they had no chance in their own country, and they hewed out homes for themselves, and many of those people who went to the States with their belongings in a little tin box many years ago are among the greatest men of that great republic. Let us remember that, for the sake of the development of the country, when a bill is brought before us we should not turn it down simply because the project does not come into our district. We cannot have a great Canada without developing our vast resources, and if these resources are developed, they will pay our public debt.
An hon. gentleman yesterday mentioned a subject very dear to my heart. I have spoken upon that question in this House several times, and a gentleman who was once in this House, but who is now in the Ontario legislature, Mr. Keefer, was very much interested in it. He had been down in the British West Indies, and other islands and had seen the great resources of the country. I may say that within my day the United States have made great accretions to their territory, through small wars, through diplomacy and a few dollars. They have enlarged their outlying districts to nearly double their former size. In the British West Indies the people

The Address-Mr. Baldwin
speak English, French and Spanish about equally. They have got the products that we require, and, instead of buying them from those countries, we have been buying a hundred million dollars worth of produce through concerns in the United States.
I saw an article stating that we had not lived up to an agreement in regard to refrigerator boats to the West Indies. At the period I mention we were buying a hundred million dollars worth of goods from the United States in tropical and semi-tropical products. They were paying the West Indies six cents for an article and selling to us for fifteen cents. Instead of going direct to that country and buying the goods from them, we are buying through the United States. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) brought that point out specifically yesterday. I was very proud of him, because he is conversant with the situation. We need their products and they need ours. We are a manufacturing country. We have the waterways and we have a means of communication with them, You will have observed that it costs practically nothing to transport logs by floating them down a great river. I have a friendly feeling toward that country which, once a little Crown colony, has now attained the status of a dominion-Newfoundland. Newfoundland should be linked up with Canada, and this could be done with the joint approval of the Mother Country, Newfoundland and ourselves. Indeed, the matter had at one time almost come to a head under the regime of Sir Mackenzie Bowell, the proposal being that Newfoundland should enter the confederation on condition of the payment to her of eight millions. An hon. member shakes his head, but that is as I understood it. In that country they have wonderful deposits of iron and coal right on the waterway to which I have referred.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How would my hon. friend cope with the ice conditions?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It has been suggested that ice-breakers be used on the St. Lawrence river so that it would be kept open. That is where the bridging of the straits of Belle Isle would come in; it would keep the ice floes from coming through the straits into the gulf, and through the influence of the gulf stream in the north the ice conditions would be further minimized. Now, the best sense in the world is common sense. The greatest school is the school of observation. Would it be beneath the dignity of those in charge of the affairs of this country to make overtures in this matter? What is this parliament for?

Is it simply a debating society? Is it a place wherein a fight may be carried on to determine who shall hold the government benches? One of the finest acts of diplomacy that could ever be attributed to a public man in Canada was that of the making of overtures to the West with a view to the building up of this country. An hon. member across the way laughs. Well, there is an hon. gentleman in front of him who said there was a revolution on in this country, but I do not admit it. There is, however, evolution; many things are evolving. Compare the situation in Canada to-day with that in the United States when the slave traffic and slavery led up to a division between the North and the South and a consequent civil war. It has been said that the nineteenth century was the century of the United States and that the twentieth century would be the century of Canada. Well so it was; Canada was getting along splendidly when along came the terrible world war. Canada did her part; the world recognized Canada as a great country in training 600,000 men and sending them to the front. We have an enormous debt, but we are big enough to pay that debt; we are big enough to shoulder the burden. It is said that many of our people are leaving and going to the United States, and in this connection I may point out that the figures submitted by the leader of the opposition showed big, because thousands of those who go across the border and pay their head tax of $S return within six months and are paid back their money. The people I would like to keep at home are the capitalists, they should go into Quebec and Ontario and open up some of our great iron mines. Look at the iron deposits that are found in the states bordering this country; look at their vast wealth. We want those men here; we do not want them down there squandering their time. We have a white population in Canada; in the United States they have 12,000,000 negroes-a question of no small account. They have had a great many lynchings down there, a condition -which is a disgrace in a civilized country, and which, I presume, they are getting away from.
It has been stated in this House that the people in the West find it difficult to make a fair realization upon capital invested in farm properties. As I said last year, it would appear that both the old political parties are'responsible, to the extent of about fifty-fifty, for the expending of $20,000,000 on the Hudson Bay railway. I have said in this House that if the Hudson Bay railway could be put into operation by the expenditure of four or five millions, I was in

The Address-Mr Baldwin
favour of it,. I represent one of the largest manufacturing counties in this Dominion. No less than three of our greatest industries are located in my county-the great Dominion Textiles, the Union Twist Drill Company, the only whip factory in Canada, and scores of other manufacturers. Now, any such expenditure as I have mentioned, in any part of this great Dominion, reflects itself in my own county. I am in favour of the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. The right hon. leader of the opposition seems to think that he will have an opportunity pretty soon of going before the people; let him come to my constituency and discuss these matters. I doubt, however, whether his expectation will be realized. I believe that this session will continue to its ordinary conclusion and that we shall have two more sessions before the federal elections come on. I would ask the leader of the opposition whether he believes that if an election took place within two weeks or two months, any larger group would come back to this House than is here now.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not on that side.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, and not on his side.
The people of Canada do not forget.
