Some man goes into the pullman with a box of cigars and treats the men in there; and, as is only natural, there are people in this country, as there are in every other country, who are subject to brainstorms once in a while, and the result is that this man obtains the consensus of opinion of the whole Dominion right in that little smoker. I did not intend to make these remarks, but as the speeches of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) are always more or less tinged with sarcasm, I thought it only proper that I should make some observations this afternoon. I think that, instead of indulging in partisan criticism, the representatives of the people in parliament should come here and direct all their energies and their eloquence to the enunciation of a policy that will promote the interests of their own communities and of the country at large as well.
I see a great and glorious future ahead of this country. The twentieth century is going to be a great one for Canada, although the last ten years of the first quarter have been rendered rather frustrate as a result of war and war conditions. But this country, notwithstanding these conditions, will prosper, and in my opinion Canada will grow to be one of the greatest nations on the face of the earth. This, however, can be possible only if our people will throw ff their coats and roll
up their sleeves and get down to work. What I am most interested in is to see a diminution in the public debt. If we had not the railway octopus to grapple with, we should no doubt have been in a fairly good position today. Some people believe in the principle of nationally owned railways, and no doubt our railways will be a tremendous asset to Canada if the present government remains in power. I' do not think that there could be found a greater business man, from the point of view of ability and experience in his own particular line, than the president of the Canadian National Railways, Sir Henry Thornton. Sir Henry Thornton has said that he will make the roads self-supporting in two or three years. I believe he will. That being the case, what better outlook do we want from the standpoint of our railways? All we need to do is so to manage the affairs of the country that we shall be able to make it possible to build branch lines to serve growing communities who are far from any means of transportation at the present time. What we want in this country is optimism, not pessimism; we do not want everlasting fighting in the House, for that is injurious to the interests of the whole country. It does not matter so much what any prime minister says; what is of importance is what the government does. And in justice to the Liberal party, this being only the third session of the present administration, is it not reasonable, sensible and businesslike that they be given a chance to administer the affairs of the country in the way a great board administers the business of an important organization? No one has ever heard of directors fighting around the board; if they did, they would soon cease to function as a body. We are placed here in trust to assist in the administration of the affairs of this Dominion, and we are neglecting our duties as representath es of the people so long as we fail to help the government, by advice and counsel, as far as we can. And the country will never prosper so long as men with the ability and the eloquence of the leader of the opposition continue to devote that ability and that eloquence to purposes other than those which will promote the interests of the people as a whole. We must give up squabbling merely to see who shall sit on the front benches. I promised when I began, Mr. Speaker, that I would not detain the House at any great length, and although there are many other matters on which I should have liked to touch, I shall bring my remarks to a close for the present.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of

The Address-Mr. Lucas
interest to the debate as it has progressed, and I am sure that others will agree with me when I say that one can come to no other conclusion than that conditions are not as they should be in Canada to-day. When we members of the West presumed last year to speak on immigration we were described as apostles of gloom. But if our utterances at that time were open to such criticism, I would ask now, what must be said of the very dismal picture that has been so graphically presented to the House by many hon. members, whom I will not name but who liave taken part in this discussion? If we Slave come to the conclusion that something is wrong, then I think we have reached the point from which we may be able to make some progress.
It seems to me that altogether too much time has been consumed in this House in the past in an attempt on the part of both of the old political parties to shoulder the blame upon each other for the conditions as they have existed in the country. During the last two sessions in which I have been in this House we have listened hour after hour to the representatives of one party trying to fasten upon the other party the responsibility for railway conditions and other unfortunate circumstances in Canada at the present time. Suppose we could definitely settle who was responsible in any of these matters, would it put us any further ahead? We should still have our present problems to solve. In my opinion, therefore, as we have all been more or less responsible for conditions as they are, we should try to forget the past and should resolve henceforth to devote our time to a solution of the problems that confront us. This is what we shall have to do if we hope to move in the right direction.
I want to congratulate the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) on the sentiments he expressed the other evening when he suggested that a political revolution was taking place in this country as elsewhere. I heartily endorse what he said on that occasion.
I want to say that we from Alberta-and I can speak only for that province-are sent to this House not for the aggrandisement or the promotion of the interests of any political party, but for the purpose of co-operating with other members, no matter from what part of Canada they come, who have at heart the best interests of the country as a whole and are anxious to see its affairs properly governed. Our friends to the right are very fond of throwing taunts at us; they tell us that we are selling our birthright to the government. Let me inform hon. gentlemen I Mr. Lucas.]
that if ever they occupy the seats of government in this House-so far as I, at least, am concerned, and I think I can speak for the other members of this group-if they bring down anything that we consider in the best interests of the whole of Canada, they will get our support as readily as the present government. When we look back over the history of the -world we see that conditions have always been changing, and we realize that the Great War, without parallel in its extent and reaction, has brought about conditions very difficult to meet. In connection with these new conditions, I was particularly struck by an article which I read a short time ago in the New Leader from the pen of Ramsay MacDonald, who is very much in the limelight at the present time as Prime Minister of Great Britain. While not in sympathy with proportional representation, he has this to say;
Ail that is necessary is that we should adapt our minds and our methods of parliamentary organization to the new conditions.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the most promising suggestion which any leading statesman has yet presented for the future political development of countries enjoying the British parliamentary system. Discussing what proportional representation might bring about Mr MacDonald writes:
The first effect will be to loosen party bonds. Members,. while holding generally to party principles and conceptions of policy, will more frequently than they do now use their own judgment as to how to vote. Parties themselves may have to change, and whilst increasing their propaganda and educational work in the country, will rule in the House of Commons more by their administrative success than by party force, whilst the legislation that will be carried will have to be more in accordance than it now too often is with publio desires outside and the course of debates inside. This will tend to curb the partisanship of parties and make them, like cabinets, more public servants than public dictators. This can be put in another way. It will weaken organization, but strengthen reason; it will make ministers more the instruments of tile general will than the captains of party horse. On balance, that will be good, but the working of the system will call for more intelligence from the democracy.
Now, world conditions have changed to such an extent since the Great War that new methods are needed to meet them, and yet we as a people are still adhering to old-time methods. A review of the history of the world shows that with the advance of civilization our system of government has had to be changed from time to time to meet changing conditions. To-day I feel sure we have got to make another step forward in order to cope successfully with the difficulties which confront us.

The Address-Mr. Lucas
New times demand new measures and new men.
The world advances, and in time outgrows the law Which in our fathers' time seemed best;
And doubtless after us some better scheme Will be worked out by wiser men than we,
Made wiser by the steady growth of truth.
I congratulate the government upon having at last, after wandering about for two sessions, found the long-sought 5 p.m. chart and compass, and I trust they will now be able to navigate the ship of state to the port of prosperity.
I was much interested last week by the address of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) in which he described the scenic beauty and natural resources of the peninsula of Gaspe, and I would detain the House for a moment while I deal with the area and potentialities of the province of Alberta and the achievements of its people. Our province stretches seven hundred and fifty miles from north to south, and its breadth from east to west varies from a hundred and eighty to four hundred miles, with a total area of 235.280 square miles, or 163,382,400 acres-an empire within an empire. Allowing for areas covered by lakes and rivers and the rough land of the eastern slope of the Rockies and other waste districts, we are still left with 82,810.400 acres that can be easily converted to profitable agriculture. And yet we find today that only ten million acres are under cultivation. During the past year we produced ini that province 167,265,084 bushels of wheat and our total production of all grains was over 305,000,000 bushels. During the past twenty-six years we have had an average yield of 19J bushels of hard and 20J bushels of winter wheat per acre. At the Chicago International Show our farmers, in open competition against the world, carried off th" following awards: In 1920, nineteen prizes and two championships; in 1921, thirty-two prizes and four championships; in 1922. thirty-six prizes and three championships; and in 1923, forty-three prizes and four championships. The results achieved have convinced us not only of the volume of grains and grasses capable of being produced in our province, but we are convinced that these stand head and shoulders above those produced in any other province or state on the North American continent. When I add that those results have been achieved by a population of less than 600,000 people. I think hon. members will agree with me that those people have every reason to be proud of their success. Year by year we realize more and more that there are no bounds to the production of wheat within Alberta. While mixed farming
forms a very important part of our agriculture in that province, yet it is patent that the cultivation of wheat is the principal money-producing crop, and will continue to develop to a greater and greater extent as the years go by.
Apart from agriculture, we have vast coal and other mineral resources. It is estimated that the total coal reserves of the province exceed one hundred billion tons, comprising 87 per cent of the coal areas of the Dominion, 72 per cent of those of the Empire, and 14 per cent of those of the world. I hope a solution of the transportation problem may be found whereby the coal of Alberta will be hauled to Ontario at a rate which will make it possible for the people'in that section to use and thus save over one hundred million dollars now paid annually to the United States, for this money would be distributed from one part of Canada to the other in labour and other costs and to this extent help us to pay our debts, particularly in the West.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I have abundantly shown that we have the ability to produce in Alberta. But what are the handicaps we are laboring under? While I may have to present a sectional viewpoint in this connection, my opinion is that what affects one part of the Dominion adversely is bound to react to the prejudice of the whole country. We in Alberta are situated on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains. We have a longer freight haul than any other part of the Dominion for our produce going out and for all the commodities that we use coming in. Now nature never intended that to be so. We find that while the Rocky mountains lie between our province and the Pacific ocean, nature has provided a pass through these mountains, and our National railway traverses them on a gradient of less than half of one per cent for the greater part of the distance, with a maximum of only seven-tenths of one per cent for a distance of some twenty-eight miles. Yet we find that we are denied that natural outlet for our products. While a reduction of tariff will have a great effect, and will no doubt help us in many ways yet I am forced to this conclusion, that one of the greatest handicaps the people of the West are labouring under to-day is the transportation difficulty, and I am sure that there is nothing this government and this parliament could do for western Canada that would give that section of the country a greater measure of satisfaction than the equalization of freight rates as between the East and the West.
The Address-Mr. Lucas

To give you an idea of the conditions we are labouring under in regard to freight rates, if you take eastern Canada at a basis of 100, the freight rates over the prairies will be represented by 120, and of British Columbia by 135. If you are going to adopt the principle of apportioning the freight rates according to the cost of construction or operation, then let us adopt that principle for the whole of Canada. When you take into consideration that the earnings on our roads in the West have greatly exceeded the earnings in the East, we are not prepared to admit that the cost of construction and operation in the West are greater than in the East. Let me give you these figures. From 1907 to 1911 the net earnings on the eastern lines amounted to $43,500,000, and on the western lines to $91,500,000, or $48,000,000 more in the West, or 110 per cent greater. From 1912 to 1916 the net earnings in the East amounted to $60,000,000, and in the West to $152,000,000, or $92,500,000 more in the West, or 154 per cent. From 1916 to 1920 the net earnings in the East amounted to $70,000,000 and in the West to $144,500,000, or $74,000,000 more in the West, or 105 per cent. In 1921 the earnings in the East amounted to $11,000,000 and in the West to $30,000,000, or $19,000,000 more in the West, or 157 per cent. Is it any wonder there is dissatisfaction in the West under this treatment?
There is a great deal of dissatisfaction in all parts of Canada to-day. We hear rumblings from the Maritime provinces, from central Canada and from the West, and certain members in this House seem to be of the opinion that we from the West are whining for some special favours. I should like to say to this House and to the people of eastern Canada that we from the West are not asking for any special favours. We are simply asking for equal opportunities, and we shall never have unity in this country unless it is founded upon a spirit of justice and equality.
In shipping our goods to our natural outlet we have what is known as the mountain rate, the export rate, and the domestic rate. For instance, we have an export rate at the present time from Calgary or Edmonton to Vancouver of 22+ cents per 100 pounds of wheat. The domestic rate is 42 cents per 100 pounds.
I have tried to get some explanation from our freight experts and others in this country as to the justification for this domestic rate, but up to the present time I have not been able to find anyone who could give me any justification for it. We find that there is no domestic rate on wheat in eastern Canada, and the result is that a farmer in the West shipping 	; i 1
two loads of wheat to Vancouver, if he ships one load to a Chinaman, and the Orient is taking a great deal of our wheat to-day, it pays an export rate of 22+ cents per 100 pounds, whereas the other load, if it is shipped to a fruit grower or a chicken farmer in British Columbia or to one of the mills there, has to pay the domestic rate of 42 cents per 100 pounds. We are evidently favouring the Chinese farmer in our freight rates, and enabling him to raise his eggs cheaper and flood this country with Chinese eggs to the disadvantage of our Canadian producers. Yet we are supposed to have a railway commission to deal with such matters.
W'hen we come to the tariff it is a question that the two old parties have fought over in this House for the last forty years and it is still about where it started. We know that the tariff has been a political football ever since confederation, I want to disabuse the minds of any hon. members of the idea that we farmers are here to put our manufacturers out of business. I do not think there is a farmer in the West who wants to see that happen. We realize that we must have manufactures in this country, but one industry cannot be built up at the expense of another, and it seems to me that the only solution of this question lies in getting together in a spirit of co-operation and endeavouring to settle this question on a strictly business basis. Only by acting in that way shall we improve our conditions.
Another great handicap we labour under in the West is the matter of credit. I do not stand before this House and say that we want more credit in the West, but just as Great Britain came to the United States a couple of years ago to make arrangements for refunding her debt, over a long period of years and at a low rate of interest, so we in western Canada to-day are simply asking you to put us in a position where we can fund our debts into one loan and spread the payments over a number of years, thereby giving us a chance to meet our obligations. We are not asking for more credit, nor is any man trying to get out of the responsibilities he has assumed at the present time, but we want to make it possible for our people to pay their debts. We see what the United States is doing to help the agriculturists of that country in the matter of credit. Within the last year they brought in a rural credit scheme, and to show you the advantage the American farmer has over the Canadian farmer in making a loan, the American can secure a time loan of say $1,000, spread over thirty-four years, at the rate of 5J per cent, which

The Address-Mr. Lucas
amortizes the loan. At the end of that period he will have paid off in principal and interest a sum amounting to $1,870. Now a farmer in Canada borrowing $1,000, and letting it run for thirty-four years, at 8 per cent-I am taking that as the general rate, although a great many of us are paying a higher rate of interest-will have paid back at the end of thirty-four years in principal and interest $3,720. Now, I think that is a handicap impossible for the Canadian farmer to overcome.
We all realize that immigration is one of the crying needs of Canada to-day. We have a country that is not equalled in any part of the world. We have vast natural resources, millions of acres of land that are yet uncultivated, and we have provided facilities for a population many times our actual number; we find a population of nine millions of people trying to carry a load which possibly twenty-five or fifty millions should support. Now, what is the problem before us. We all agree that our people are leaving the Dominion. Is the problem before us to spend money in going out and seeking to bring in others to take their places, or should it be our main object to try and get together, find out what is responsible for that exodus, and other evils and then provide the remedy. I believe there is no comparison between a Canadian born and bred in this country and any foreigner who may be brought in to take his place. And yet we find to-day that our Canadian born sons and daughters are leaving this country, and instead of spending money to find out what is causing this exodus, we are making expenditures on an immigration policy and flooding Europe with advertisements to attract foreign born settlers to Canada.
There is one thing we must recognize. That is that Canada is a hard country to govern. Stretching as it does from o'cean to ocean, with so many divergent conditions in different parts of the country, we must adopt a broad outlook. Having realized the position we are in, we shovdd adopt a different policy from that which has been followed in the past. We should discard the idea of considering, when a question is introduced in the House, whether it will be in the interest of a party, whether it will keep a party in power, or enable a party to get into power. We must forget all ideas of that kind, and try to evolve a policy that will be in the interest of the country as a whole.
There is one other question to which I would like to refer. It has been in my mind for some time, and it was brought out the other day when the hon. member for Centre
Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) -was speaking of the judiciary. I am merely going to throw the suggestion out to the government and hon. members. I believe we all want to see the judiciary occupy a status high above any possibility of reflection. I want to make it quite plain at the present time that I am not casting any reflection upon our judges; but I think they should be in such a position that there would be no possibility of reflecting upon them in any manner whatever. Therefore I should like to see the appointment of judges taken out of the hands of the government and no longer continue to be a matter of political patronage. It seems to me that appointments to the judiciary could very well be left to the bar associations in the various provinces throughout the Dominion. I feel sure that the lawyers in our various provinces have enough pride in their profession to see to it that none but the very best men would be selected to sit on the bench in a judicial capacity. At the present time it is very often felt whether rightly or not, that a man is rewarded to a seat on the bench because of his political activities, I do not think it is in the best interest of the country as a whole that this should continue to be the case.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say there is no argument in regard to the wonderful character of our country. We have a land that will provide bountifully for millions: We have a class of people that, when they go to other countries, can hold their own in competition with anyone. It seems to me therefore that if we would just use a little of the common sense that the Almighty Las endowed us with, and get together here not as men from the East or from the West but as Canadians assembled in parliament, and wipe away much of this party prejudice from our minds, we could solve the problem that confronts us and by so doing make of Canada a prosperous and contented land, and a land to love.
Mr. C. II. DICKIE (Nanaimo):	Mr. Speaker at the outset I wish to associate myself with those who preceded me in tendering congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I also, in common with other hon. members, deplore the absence of one so universally and respectfully esteemed as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding).
I regret very much, Mr. Speakfer, to see omitted from the Speech any suggestion of any legislative action whatever with respect
The Address-Mr. Dickie

to the retention within our Dominion of our forest reserves. I think, Sir, this is a question of immense importance to our country. It is quite possible that owing to the fact that a commission, an expensive commission, is at present touring the country and inquiring into the obvious, that the government does not care to make a pronouncement on this question until the findings of the commission are at hand. Otherwise I consider their conduct is inexcusable, in view of the very great blunder that is being perpetrated by the failure to protect our country by preventing the exportation of our raw forest products. The commission in question was sitting in British Columbia prior to my departure; I presume it is sitting there still. Owners of timber lands, American tugboat owners, and others engaged in logging were giving evidence against the imposition of an embargo upon the exportation of raw material. That those who were profiting by exportation should be against the imposition of an embargo was naturally to be expected and was the case. As usual the general public of British Columbia. paid little attention to the commission, and I can safely say, through long residence in that country, and familiarity with the conditions, economic and otherwise, that were the matter subject to a plebiscite, 85 per cent of the people of British Columbia would vote for an embargo to prevent the exportation of saw logs from our country. Those logs are leaving our country at an ever accelerating rate, and we are alarmed at the rapid depletion of our forests. All talk of reforestation with Douglas fir is futile and nonsensical. The difficulties in the way of renewing the forest growth of our country are absolutely insuperable. We see our logs going, day by day, in immense booms across the border, to enrich our neighbours, and our young men are following there, to engage in the manufacture of them. We are harvesting the last crop of Douglas fir from our mountain side, and leaving behind a scene of desolation that is hard to describe. I remember once noticing a picture of Dante's Inferno by Gustave Dore which very fairly represents what the countryside looks like after being logged over. If the harpies were present the resemblance would be complete. In 1920 we exported in round numbers 28,000,000 feet of lumber in the form of saw logs from British Columbia. In 1921 we exported 90,000.000 feet and in 1922, 151,000,000. In 1923 we exported 233,000,000 feet. There are reasons for expecting that the figures will run to approximately 500,000,000 in 1924. It should be apparent to all that in the interests of the present, to  .
say nothing of the coming generation, we must at least see to it that our timber is manufactured within the confines of our country; and even then we are perhaps cutting too freely. Let "festina lente "[DOT]-make haste slowly-be our motto with respect to harvesting our timber and even our generation will profit thereby and will bless us.
Just prior to leaving the West I was credibly informed that eight standard sawmills were being or about to be erected on Puget Sound waters just south of the International boundary line. What is termed a standard mill will cut 250,000 feet of lumber per day. The eight mills in question would cut 500 million feet yearly, and it is obvious to those familiar with forestry conditions in that country that British Columbia is being looked to almost entirely for a log supply. You can easily see what a deplorable situation this is. To bring the enormity of our immense log exportation more clearly before you, let me say that the total lumber cut of New Brunswick in 1923 was 265 million feet, and surely every person, especially those from the Maritime provinces, will realize the great importance of the lumbering industry in that province. We next year will export twice that many logs, I have good reason to expect, to our American cousins.
Dr. Mayo of Boehester, Minnesota, in a recent address given under the auspices of the Canadian Club at Victoria, B.C., strongly impressed on his audience the immense importance of conserving our forests, saying that the^ people of his state were now realizing their folly in allowing the slaughter of their forests in one generation. A very substantial company from the southern states has recently acquired a tract of timber in British Columbia estimated at 3,000 million feet. Before leaving for the south to complete arrangements for operating, Mr. Jasspan, the company's manager, said in part;
The depletion of our southern forests is a calamity for which this and coming generations will suffer.
He also said:
We do not contemplate entering into the sawmill business, we will sell our logs.
The logs in question, Mr. Speaker, will doubtless go across the line. The Financial Post of February 29, has this to say with respect to the momentous question of timber exports:
The Ontario legislature will be asked to approve of legislation placing an embargo on the exportation of hardwood from the province. The measure is designed to force United States plants in Minnesota and Wisconsin to cross into Ontario to manufacture their pro-

The Address-Mr. Dickie
ducts if they desire to use Ontario hardwood. The measure is similar to the pine embargo of some years ago. That measure resulted in many saw mills locating in the north. There are about 1,300 hardwood plants located in Wisconsin and Minnesota. Henry Ford entered the area and purchased practically all the available reserves. The estimate made to-day is that the end of seven years will see but 100 to 110 of these plants remaining because of the exhaustion of their supply of raw material. Realizing this there has been a rush into Algoma, United States concerns have eagerly sought control of the available limits on the Canadian side. It is understood that one American concern made a contract to ship 100 million feet of hardwood across lake Superior. This was to have gone to the Iron Mountain plant of Henry Ford. Ontario's reserves of hardwood , are limited. The estimate is that the small area in which hardwood thrives contains 6,500 million feet. This includes the big forest reserve and runs north to the border of the clay-belt. In discussing the embargo, Hon. James Lyons, Ontario s Minister of Lands and Forests, pointed out that some years ago the numerous saw mills around Saginaw and Bay City, Michigan, were importing Canadian logs heavily An embargo was placed on their exportation with the result that there is $75,000,000 invested in saw mills around the Soo to-day. The Canadian Pacific railway line, Soo to Sudbury, is studded with them. He also points out that in 1900 there was an embargo m regard to pulp with the result that $190,000,000 are invested in the pulp plants of the provmce to-day.
This, Mr. Speaker, is my case against the exportation of saw logs. I have been fair in my arguments and if the House believes my statements, surely the hour is at hand when we will cease temporizing with this deplorable situation.
Now a few words with respect to pulpwood exports, although I confess at the outset that I am not as familiar with this question as with the one I have just dealt with. Pulp-wood exportation is just commencing in British Columbia and I hope to see it strangled at birth. In 1923 there was exported from the Dominion to the United States pulpwood to the value of thirteen million dollars. Had this pulpwood been manufactured into paper it would have had a value of ninety million dollars, seventy million at least of which would have gone to labour, to people who live in our country, people who purchase the
products of our farms and of our factories, people who would help to build up our nation. Instead of that this pulpwood has gone across the line to our neighbours; Surely this is bad policy for Canada.
What wonder, Mr. Speaker, that we are considered by our southern neigbours who are playing with us as a cat plays with a mouse, to be simple, non-progressive, credulous people, when in addition to errors which I have enumerated, we are going to lower our tariff barrier to those who say to us in terms that all who run may read, "We want nothing from you primitive people but your manhood, your money, and your raw forest products".
Have we no economic sense? Have we no sense of national dignity; no national pride?
I have no word of criticism of the business methods of the Americans. I have the utmost respect for their business acumen. Let us profit by their example. Let us pull ourselves together, sit up and take notice, and subscribe to the sentiments as expressed in the old Loyalist toast, "Here's to my country, may she ever be right, but right -or wrong, my country".
Still we are a credulous people and we are buying too freely from those people. We have a balance of trade from Great Britain, our best friends in a business sense. We simply add millions to that balance of trade and pass it over to our neighbours south of the line.
We all know that the mid-western farmer is penalized to a certain extent because of tariff, but in the province from which I come we absolutely could not exist without the tariff. Our manufacturers, hundreds of them, five hundred in Vancouver, would have to go out of business if there was not a substantial tariff. We are side by "side with a strong industrial nation which could afford to give away in Canada one-tenth of their product in order to put our people out of business, whereupon their prices would again go up. Our farmers and our fruit. raisers in British Columbia are in just as serious straits as you are in the West. Fruit comes in from the Wenatchee, Cashmere and Yakima valleys to the south of us a little earlier than our fruit is available. Their berries come in earlier and our market is flooded. In other words these products are dumped in on us and dumped in on the prairies before those who have expended many millions in our country can get their fruit on the market. That is the competition which the people in the Okanagan country have to meet.
Speaking about hardships on the prairies reminds me of the story of two men who were fishing in a lake in British Columbia and who saw a man struggling in the water at the foot of a cliff. They pulled toward him as rapidly as they could and succeeded in rescuing him. After some fishermen's supplies had been administered to him he sat up, looked at his watch, and said; "Will you put me ashore? I am behind with my work. This is the third time this morning that I have fallen off my ranch." These are the things the farmers have to contend with in some parts of British Columbia. On the prairies a man does not have to be an amphibian to farm.
I regret very much to hear any talk about secession coming from hon. gentlemen to my left. I do not think that is the feeling that

The Address-Mr. Dickie
permeates the middle West. I do not like to hear this talk of the sound of a breeze going through the tops of the mulberry trees, or anything that smacks of a feeling that we are not going to be a united people. Let us forget all this racial and religious talk; let us realize that we all have our troubles. The Maritime provinces undoubtedly suffer because of our tariff policy; well, we can make up for that by giving them a quid pro quo. We certainly can give a quid pro quo to my neighbours to the left; there are ways in which we can more than make up to them what they lose through the tariff, as was so ably pointed out by the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) this afternoon. I say with certainty that we in British Columbia could not exist-the farmers could not exist, the manufacturers could not exist, without a suitable tariff. The same can pretty well be said about Ontario and Quebec. With the Maritime provinces it is different, and it is different with you people in the West, but surely there is some way by which we can get on common ground, and avoid taking any step which, while giving comparatively small benefit to the western people, would sacrifice the manufacturing industries of Ontario and Quebec.
We have all read the startling articles in MacLean s Magazine with regard to what may be termed the '"pork barrel" argument. Part of one of those articles contained an attack on my friend from Victoria City (Mr.Tolmie). It is stated that a dry-dock was promised to Victoria as a bribe to elect that hon. gentleman. Sir, that is unqualifiedly false, because that dry-dock was promised years before the member for Victoria City entered political life. The member for Victoria City did not need to offer a dry-dock as a bonus to bring about his election. He is a well known native son of that province and I believe he could be elected in any British Columbia constituency without giving a dry-dock or anything else. Moreover, the dry-dock is not in the constituency of the hon. member for Victoria City, it is in mine. I only hope that when this gentleman writes other articles of that kind he will keep a little nearer to the facts, because he has done an injustice. A branch of the Yarrow shipbuilding firm was located in Esquimalt long before the member for Victoria City ever thought of politics or was thought of by others in that regard. Subsequently the Yarrow firm started there because of assurance that a dry-dock would be built and are now doing an immense business. They have ships there all the time and they will have larger ships when the dry-dock is big enough for them. fMr. Dickie.] .
It was stated also in this "pork barrel'' article that there already was in that district a dry-dock 265 feet long. The dry-dock is 230 feet long, and I know of six or seven war ships which during the troublous days of the war had to go to the American side to be docked because the facilities in British Columbia were not adequate. Our friends in Vancouver, of course, do not feel the same enthusiasm for a dry-dock as I do. I think, however, that with the rapid strides that are being made in that wonderful city of Vancouver, in two or three years there will be room for two or more big dry-docks in British Columbia. There are sixteen large dry docks to the south of us on the American side, and the opportunities of shipping coming into our country or going through our ports on the way to American ports are undoubtedly very great.
I was rather amused by some figures quoted by the very gentlemanly speaker from Montreal by way of proof that, the exodus of people from Canada during the last two years was no greater than it had been during the two preceding years. That shows what can be done with figures. The hon. member must know, or he should know, that such a conclusion is absurd. Everybody knows, even the boy on the street, that during this last year the exodus to the States more than doubled that of the two preceding years. We in British Columbia do not know where to look for young men. They are going down to southern California, and there are very good reasons for that: unexampled prosperity reigns down there owing to the development of immense oil wells and other activities. Now these people are coming back, but only very slowly. I do not think the exodus will continue for any considerable time, but before we can stamp it out, before we can do anything to make this the country that we want it to be, we must have what has been mentioned time after time, namely, stability of tariff regulation. The people must know where they are at. Those who come from the West must realize that, in view of w'hat they have heard. They heard it from the hon. member (Mr. Hams) who spoke last night, and who told how men engaged in industry in Toronto, industry in which hundreds of thousands of dollars had been invested, had during the last two or three years worked with their overalls on, fought with their backs to the wall, to make this a prosperous country. Still you gentlemen would lower the tariff. If you give the question the thought that it deserves I am sure that you will arrive at the conclusion that there is some other way of meeting the situa-

The Address-Mr. MacLaren
tion than by lowering the tariff and sacrificing the interests of Quebec and Ontario.
In conclusion, I would simply plead that we forget sectionalism, that we forget this talk of secession. We are one people, a British people, and Canadians above all. We have our difficulties. We have our racial dividing lines, though they do not prevail in the West. In the constituency that I am trying to represent we have many French Canadians and they are among the best people we have-
I would we had more of them. They still hold to the teachings that they imbibed at their mother's knee, in the matter of religion and everything else, and I give them crediit for it. They are men, too, who take an active part in our public life out there. I may say,. Mr. Speaker, that although I am a Conservative every one of these people voted for me in my constituency. I do not think that there is anything further that I care to say at the present time.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Mr. MURRAY MacLAREN (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject which I desire to discuss is to be found in the thirteenth paragraph of the Speech from the Throne. It is the shortest paragraph and deals with the development of Canadian trade through Canadian seaports. The Prime Minister in his speech did not refer to this important subject, but I hope it will receive in inverse proportion the attention which it has received up to the present time. He brushed aside the significance of the recent reverses to his party in the East by saying that they were due to sectional issues. Sectional issues! Our experience is that such issues receive the greatest attention at the hands of the government. To that land of sections and half sections, the prairie provinces, the Crowsnest pass agreement was offered last year; this year a reduction of the tariff on the instruments of production is promised; and next year or in the near future, should the government continue in power, the West will probably have its hopes revived in that Utopian vision, the Hudson Bay railway. The promise of its completion will be brought in on a charger and presented to the Progressive party. The leader of that party has already said, as have his supporters also, that this project must be carried out. Not only is the Progressive party the life and breath of the government, but it has now assumed to act as the administration's mouthpiece. I
can readily understand that when a government has to contend with assaults from without as well as from within its vitality is likely to be very much weakened. Indeed, its vitality is now at a very low ebb, and the further discussion of this question has apparently been handed over by the government, appropriately enough, to the vigorous lepresentatives of the northwestern provinces.

speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me? He must not get his leader in wrong. Does he not know that the right hon. gentleman has declared himself in favour of the Hudson Bay railway?

speechtext: I am trying to represent the .views contained within myself.

The assaults within the
party.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Fortunately a great
many men on this side of the House have views of their own and are quite capable of expressing them. I am presenting my own view, and I am not alone in entertaining it.
I tried to get an expression of opinion from the Minister of Railways last year with regard to the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, but, unlike my leader, he apparently held no opinion on the subject, at least he failed to give expression to any. These reverses of the government were not due to sectional issues but were largely due to questions of transportation which I am now discussing.
I listened yesterday with very careful attention to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), and I desire to say that many of the important subjects he dealt with received my complete acquiescence. I would refer first of all to the British preference. For many years we had a statute providing that British imports must be made through Canadian ports before the preference would become effective. This law was to be put into force by order in council, but it was never promulgated. Last year, it will be remembered, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) introduced a motion providing for a 10 per cent preference on a large number of British commodities, subject to one condition, that they be brought in through our ports. This was an acknowledgement of an important principle and was, I think, an advance on the tariff legislation that had been enacted up to that time. But after all, it is really a nibbling at the question. It is ten per cent. To be plain about the matter the figures at the present time are not conclusive because the time has been too short to prepare the statistics bear-

The Address-Mr. MacLaren
ing on the point, but the belief is that even the ten per cent has had considerable influence in increasing Canadian trade through Canadian seaports. I would join with the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) in urging that the motion as previously passed by this House should, be readopted and put into force, so that all goods receiving the preference must come through Canadian channels. I see this further advantage in it; it does hot disturb the tariff. You have a tariff, and then it is interfered with by inserting the ten per cent, but if it applies generally to all goods imported through Canadian ports, only the tariff is not disturbed.
Then there is the matter of ttade with the West Indies. That, I think, was well put before the House by the hon. member. There is an opportunity for this country to benefit to a vastly greater extent than it does at the present time by the proper adjustments of duties and tariffs.
Then as to coal production in Canada. The bringing in of a policy that would be so arranged that we would be independent of any other country for our supply of coal is one of the important questions of the day. I cannot but think that the making of much greater use of our own coal than we are doing at the present time is well within our possibilities. I noticed that the hon. member for Cumberland was in favour of a duty upon bituminous coal somewhat higher than the present duty. He was careful to point out that this was not protection for the coal, but simply a tariff for revenue. What he wants is a duty on bituminous coal for revenue, for the purpose of giving protection. Now the difficulty with many members is that certain duties are perfectly all right and advantageous provided you do not put a protectionist label on them. To my mind it makes no difference at all whether you attach the name protection or not if you put the duty on, and if the hon. member for Cumberland is satisfied with that kind of designation I do not think we need worry very much about it. The result and the effect are there.
Now, a word about what was called the old Intercolonial railway. According to my understanding, the Intercolonial railway is not an integral part of the Canadian National Railways. I believe that the accounting is kept separate, and it is kept separate because the government regard it as on a different basis.
I believe that under the British North America Act, technically speaking, it is not and cannot be a portion of the Canadian National Railways. Then there is the Railway Commission. The Railway Commission, cannot deal with

the rates on that portion of the system called the Intercolonial railway. As a matter of fact, it is somewhat of an academic question. The Intercolonial is operated and managed with the Canadian National Railways as a matter of convenience, and because it is a matter of considerable advantage, I believe, from many points of view. That is my interpretation of the Intercolonial question. I am not sure that I have satisfied the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) on that point, but be that as it may, I think my view is put forward with considerable accuracy.
Now I come to the Canadian National Railways, and I am pleased to see the Minister of Railways in his seat. It seems to me that there is a great deal of what may be termed loose thinking and loose speaking about the relationship between the Canadian National Railway board, the government and the country. The government says a good deal along this line: We will give the railway board a free hand. Now that is an inaccurate expression, and in a matter where it is so important to define the exact relationship between the railway board, the country, and the government, I think we should have something more explicit than simply the words "a free hand." Under the act the railway board is appointed for the operation and management of these railways; for the operation and management, that is all. I presume, then, that if you say it has a free hand, it is a free hand under the conditions as expressed, that is, in the operation and management. But the board, if you read the act, is also subject to conditions and restrictions as imposed by the Governor in Council. The government, however, have imposed no conditions and no restrictions through order in council, and none are filed in that office. In other words, the government have not exercised any supervision or given any directions to the railway board. I do not mean that there should be small restrictions; I mean something above and higher than the question of operation and management. There is an opportunity there, and I presume that when the act was drawn it was put there for that purpose, in order that the government could exercise its functions on the higher ground of the best policy having regard to the conditions of the country, and that that idea be expressed and conveyed to the railway board.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Is there any
provision in the act which puts that responsibility upon the government?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The act states thri the board has conveyed to it the operation and management of the railways. I say that the government has the power of limiting, of re-

The Address

Mr. MacLaren
stricting, of supervising the action of the railway board. It is laid down so in the act, and here there is an opportunity for the government to express a high policy regarding the greater matters of transportation in this country. I also say there has been, up to the present, no such policy conveyed to the railway board. It is not necessary of course, for the government to do that; they may have no policy. I presume they have not or they would so express it. In reality, one looks on the railway board as an organization which should not be interfered with in any way in matters that come legitimately within their powers unless, of course, something occurs which must be criticized. Politics must not enter into the management, but no one wishes that politics should enter there. I did not know where to place my hon. friend from Cumberland yesterday when he spoke of indirect appointments by the government to the railway system. That is a matter a little too vague in character to try and enlighten the House upon.
Now, as I say, while the government has this authority to condition, it is not free to take any policy it sees fit regarding the railways. The railway board is subject to the government, and the government is subject to the statutes that have been previously passed by parliament, and that I believe is a very important point. The government itself is not free; it is limited by statutes which have previously passed parliament. I should therefore ask what these railway acts are. My hon. friend (Mr. Logan) yesterday referred to them, and said that some of the provisions had come within his knowledge only within the last few weeks. This to us is somewhat surprising as he is looked upon as the defender of the rights of the Maritime provinces. If it be true in his case there are probably many other members of the House who are not familiar with these acts. I therefore ask hon. members to refer to the acts in question and see exactly what is contained therein. I will not attempt to quote them, I did so last year, but I again draw the attention of the House to three acts in particular. One is the National Transcontinental Railway Act of 1903, another is the Act respecting aid toward the construction of the Canadian Northern Railway of 1911, and the third is the Act respecting the Canadian Northern Railway System of 1914. These acts were passed during the periods of both the Liberal government and the Conservative government. There is no way by which the present government' or the opposition can decline to accept responsibility for one or more of them.
If hon. members will take the opportunity of reading these statutes they will be surprised, I believe, at all they contain. They may vary in degree, but even the powers conveyed by one or any of the three are very great and would have an enormous influence on the trade of this country. They all lay down that unrouted freight is to be passed over our Canadian railways to Canadian seaports. Large financial assistance, in some cases enormous financial assistance, was granted these railroads and m return the companies undertook to do certain things. You will find the conditions all set forth in the statutes, but for one thing they undertook that unrouted freight should be forwarded over Canadian railways to Canadian ports with a view of building up a great national policy regarding transportation in this country. That being the case, when the government took over the system of railroads it took over the commitments as well as the lines. Therefore I would submit that under all Canadian governments the control and conduct of our railway system must be subject to what is contained in these three acts. I have never heard any member of the government refer to this matter, nor do I know how the government view this question. I ask the Minister of Railways-I would ask the Prime Minister if he were present-to take the opportunity of giving the House and the country a clear statement regarding this matter. Does or does not the government consent to and accept these commitments as authoritative and as governing the actions of the railway board and themselves in the management and operation of these railways? Will the Minister of Railways convey to the public his interpretation? I think it is fair to ask for it. If it be-the view of the government that these matters are authoritative, and therefore capable of being put in action, that is something that will affect the interests of our country to a very great degree. If by any chance, on the other hand, it does not appeal to the minister, I can assure him that the country will demand it. It is a request which is considered right, and the people are looking for the fulfilment of these promises and conditions. It is more than a simple matter of an agreement or contract between the railways and the government, it is also really the assent of parliament to a great policy. When those acts were adopted this House was assenting to the policy being laid down and being accepted, that transportation so far as possible should be over our Canadian rails and through our Canadian ports.

The Address-Mr. MacLaren
I think the attitude of everyone in this country towards the railway board and towards the National Railways should be a friendly one. I myself am a believer in nationally owned railways, and in any case, whether one is or is not a believer in them, I think our attitude should be friendly and one of support to the railway board. That does not mean that one must not, especially in parliament, take the opportunity of criticizing, if he thinks there is a fair opportunity for criticism. I think we should be rather unready to criticize, because technical knowledge is required on that board, and We probably do not know all the details; but still there are occasions I think when anyone will see that it is proper to criticize. I must not forget that it may be also proper to commend. I think one should not have any small spirit in the matter, and when one sees reason for commending the railway board I think he should do so. I do not say there is not an opportunity-I think there have been opportunities-for commending the railway board. The chairman of the railway board, Sir Henry Thornton, makes speeches occasionally throughout the country. He made one in December of last year in Toronto before a body of commercial travellers, and the report of the meeting states that it was unusually largely attended. I think one should be careful at all times, but should be especially careful when addressing a body such as commercial travellers, alert men, who are travelling all over the country; and if a statement is made to these travellers by someone holding the position of chairman of the railway board, that statement will go all over the country. If it is not quite correct, then there is a lot of misinformation disseminated. What did Sir Henry Thornton say to the commercial travellers in Toronto? He referred to many subjects, but came finally to the section where I have the honour to live, the Maritime provinces, and the report states:-
The great complaint he recognized had come from the Maritime provinces. They said that they were being discriminated against. Sir Henry could not see that the Maritime provinces had any complaint.
Mr. MoMASTER: He must know very little about them.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is a fair inference, but I do not know. He has had an opportunity. Surely he has had the opportunity of conversing with Maritime men and with some of the representatives of the government who come from the Maritime provinces and yet he says, that as far as he can

make out, the Mad times had little to complain about. I think a little .less speaking and a little more listening is a-
Mr. MoMASTER:	A prescription that
might be followed.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, but an aphorism that many men could apply to themselves with great advantage. We come to one more speech by the chairman of the railway board, and this speech was delivered in Montreal in February last. He was speaking at the St. James Literary Society, and he spoke again on various questions affecting transportation and railway matters of the day, and at the end of his address one of the audience brought a great many points before him, and especially as to how the railway was failing to work out properly in the Maritime provinces, and Sir Henry said:
As for the Maritime provinces, I frankly do not know what to do. I do know that it is time the rest of us got together to find a remedy for the discontent of the people down there.
Now we have heard the two statements, and it may be that he has received further information since he made his Toronto speech, but be that as it may, he says that he does not know -what to do, but that something should be done, and he thinks the matter should be taken up seriously. Now that being the position Sir Henry Thornton finds himself in, I presume he has made a report to the government on this point. It would seem a natural and proper thing to report to the government what he had found and that he did not know what to do. He knows there is cause for complaint and thinks that action should be taken. If he has not represented that matter to the government, I would suggest to the government that they inquire from him what means he would1 suggest to bring about a better condition of affairs.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to illustrate one cause of great dissatisfaction not only in the Maritimes, but over large sections of the country, and it is in reference to the grain traffic through Portland, Maine. There they are, the cities of Halifax and St. John, not very far from the city of Portland and what do we find? In November and December of 1923, and January of 1924, through Portland, Maine, and conveyed over the National railways, were 6,831,294 bushels of wheat. At the same time during the corresponding months, November and December of last year and January of this year, through the port of St. John, over the Canadian National railways, were conveyed 458,168 bushels of wheat.

The Address-Mr. MacLaren
We find nearly seven million bushels of wheat going through Portland, Maine, as against less than five hundred thousand through the port of St. John; and yet the chairman of the
(railway board says at one time in Toronto that he does not know what the cause of dis-. content in this matter is. Here, as I am pointing out to you is a very much larger amount of grain passing over Canadian rails through to Portland, Maine, over the National railways, as compared with that which passed through St. John. That, I submit, unless it has been specially routed, should go through Canadian ports. The Canadian government and the Canadian railways Eire bound by statute to encourage as much as possible the passage of grain over Canadian rails through our own ports, and discourage the passage of grain over our rails to foreign ports. Here apparently is shown that at present the provisions contained in the statutes that I have already referred to are not being observed. To show that there is more in this matter than might appear and that the main objection is not found in financial considerations, I would point out that the Canadian Pacific Railway during the same period have sent some millions of bushels of grain through the port of St. John. They are not doing it for amusement; they are doing it as a matter of business.
There is a splendid opportunity for the government to bring about, by vigorous action, a very considerable improvement in our trade. The advantage of the Imperial preference which applies only to Canada, the development of trade with the West Indies, the enforcement of the provisions contained in the acts I have spoken of-these are matters which if taken up in a vigorous way by an active government will remedy many of the conditions of which we have been complaining and will bring population and produce wealth. I cannot but think that the government is showing a masterly inactivity in these matters. I cannot see that any effort is being put forward. Only through the efforts of a strong and aggressive government, determined to carry out the tasks that lie before it, will the country take that position which I believe it should ultimately reach.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last session of this parliament various members of the group to which I adhere drew upon themselves and upon the group as a whole the adverse criticism that they were continually crying blue ruin. I have followed this debate very closely and I take it from my observations that the 16
party to my right, the official opposition, have pre-empted to themselves rights of a similar nature for this session. I have no wish to trespass on their premises, and in order that my remarks, which otherwise might be construed to be a criticism of existing conditions, may be such as to give them a bright beginning, I am going to attempt to find some ray of sunshine in that black cloud the pres-sence of which has been made the subject of reference by members on both sides of this House: I refer to the fact that we are losing many of our people, month by month and year by year.
It is pretty difficult, Mr. Speaker, to find any consolation in that fact, particularly when, as I understand, there have been months during the past year when we lost more people from our country than we had come into it. But I would point out for the consolation of the government that in losing these people we are losing many of those who are most discontented, and that, perhaps, is making the government of this country very much easier than it would be if those people remained here. I suggest that if those who were discontented had stayed in Canada there would have been more blue ruin talk and more calamity howling during this session than there has been in sessions in the past.
It is with the conditions that are causing people to leave this country that I am particularly concerned and regarding which I wish to speak for a short time this evening. I wish to analyze those conditions as far as I can-or some of them; I would not attempt to deal with them all-and to offer a few suggestions which in my estimation would tend to the betterment of those adverse conditions.
I have noted four things which I think may be called causes to which may be attributed a good proportion of the undesirable conditions which exist not in my constituency alone, not in western Canada alone, but in all of Canada which can be called agricultural-and I am sure that that is a very large percentage of the country. I will name the four conditions that I wish to deal with: first, the low prices prevailing for farm produce; second, the high costs of the necessities of life and the implements of production; third, transportation costs, and fourth, taxation. I am not sure that I have given them in their order of relative importance, but I do not think that matters very much; I shall discuss them in the order in which I have taken them.
I wish to place on record a few figures which, I must admit, are already on record and available to every member of this House.

242	'	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Stewart (Humboldt)
I have taken them from the proceedings of the special Agricultural committee which was convened last year under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master). They are enlightening, and although not strictly up to date yet I am confident that they will bear out the comparison I desire to make. First of all I will offer comparative figures for prices of grains, farm animals, and farm produce in general. Take wheat, our greatest export crop, and compare the figures of the average prices for 1913 with those of 1922, which are the years given in the table I have before me. I may say that this table was prepared by the Bureau of Statistics and was simply placed on record by the committee I have mentioned. In 1913 the average price of wheat was 67 cents-I am not sure on just what basis that price was given; in 1922 it was 85 cents, an increase of 27 per cent in those ten years. Taking oats and making the same comparison for the same years, we find the price rising from 32 to 38 cents, an increase of 18-!, per cent, and for barley the increase was from 42 to 46 cents, an increase of 9 *- per cent. Then, turning to farm animals and taking as an example western butcher steers on the Winnipeg market, in 1913 the average price per hundredweight was $6.37 and in 1922 it was $5.02, a decrease of 21 per cent. Taking hogs for the same years, but on the Toronto market, the increase between 1913 and 1922 would be shown as 28 per cent, but comparing the average price for 1913 with the price now being paid on that same market, a decrease is shown of 15 per cent. Take beef hides: in 1913 the average price was 14 cents and in 1922 it was 12,1 cents, or a decrease of 11 -3, per cent. And if, Sir, we had taken either the year 1920 or 1921, for comparative purposes, with the year 1913, that decrease would have been very much greater. Taking butter, in the year, 1913, the average price was 23| cents. In 1922, it was 31 cents, an increase of 33 per cent. Eggs show an increase of 34 per cent; and in reference to horses, which are not marketed in the usual way I have taken an extract from The Livestock News, issued by the Department of Agriculture of Saskatchewan for the month of February, 1924, which states, "The horse market is very quiet, there being a reasonable demand for good, sound, young draft horses, of from 1,400 to 1,800 pounds, at prices quoted from $100 up. Unsound, thin or undersized - omes, are practicr'ly unsaleable." The whole table, ae prepared by the Bureau of Statistics, is found to include practically all the produce that comes not only from the western farms, but from all 
the farms in Canada, and the average increase for the ten years I have cited for comparative purposes is 17 per cent. I would ask hon. members to bear that figure in mind because it has a vital relation to other figures which I shall submit. The increase in farm produce has been in the neighbourhood of 17 per cent over pre-war years. I have not quoted the extreme examples for the reason I stated when I began my remarks. But I do want to place on record what I consider an example of a condition that exists and which directly illustrates the undesirable circumstances which prevail at present among our farmers. I want to point out, however, that this is rather an extreme case. I have here a bill from the union stock yards in St. Boniface, Winnipeg, with regard to a cow that was sold there on the 19th November, 1923. Before I proceed further, let me say that I made inquiries concerning the beast in question and satisfied myself that the animal was not an exceptional one. It is true that it was not a choice beef animal, but I was assured by a score of farmers who had seen it that it was of the class of beef that is usually consumed on the farm and which, as many hon. members of this House are aware, makes a really good and substantial meal for anyone who enjoys a good farm dinner. True, this animal was sold on the wrong market; but the results are as I shall state them now. The weight of this cow was 1,140 pounds and I would point out to those who are not intimately acquainted with beef animals that any cow of this weight is not all skin and bones. The price paid in that market for this animal was 75 cents per hundred-weight, and the gross price was $8.55. From this, there had to be deducted expenses, charged up to the shipper, including freight, feed, insurance, commission, and so forth, amounting to 74.22 cents per hundredweight, making a total of $8.46. In addition to that there was another charge against the animal on account of packers' insurance of four cents, making a grand total in charges of $8.50. That meant a net return of 5 cents.

Pay to the order of....five cents only.
