maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think,
Sir, the standard difference is 10 per cent. I would not make the statement positively, but I think that is what the difference amounts to.
Then I would make a plea for the practice of economy in the utilization of labour. It is a criticism that can be brought against many of our farmers that they have followed the line of least resistance in that respect rather than hewing out a line for themselves under which they could utilize expensive labour and employ it to the very best advantage. On the other hand you may remind me that there are hundreds, indeed thousands of farmers who have followed out every point that I have

enjoined here and have found that it has helped, as I think it will help in all cases, but that it has not wholly solved the problem.
Another thing is the care of expensive implements. We have heard complaint made in that regard with respect to farmers and I think it is a just criticism. Another thing I would suggest in the line of personal endeavour would be to look carefully after the capital investment, to see that new investment is made in something that will be directly productive, particularly at this time when every cent must be earning another cent.
Another thing to which I attach great importance is carefulness in regard to the control of noxious Weeds. I may say, Mr. Speaker, there is no one item coming under the personal control of a farmer which is more important, and which if carefully attended to gives better returns than the control of noxious weeds on the farm. Still there are a great many farmers who have taken every step possible in this respect, who have kept their farms just as clean as it is possible for them' to do, and yet they find it is warfare to the bitter end with them,-that their owr personal endeavours cannot entirely overcome this particular difficulty. Here I want tc diverge long enough to draw the attention of the government to the fact that this is something they can help in. The Minister of Agriculture, I observe, is in his seat and I hope he will pay attention to my statements as they are addressed particularly to him at this time. There are sections in western Canada, as I know it, where noxious weeds are becoming a great menace, and in those same sections there are still areas of Crown lands that are administered by the government, some of it in fact held directly by the government. I have already mentioned that some farmers have made a very great fight against these weeds and have conquered them so far as their own farms are concerned; but they cannot go out on the Crown lands and achieve the same success there. That would be an utter impossibility at the present time so far as labour and the resulting cost is concerned; and I ask you, Sir, if it is not reasonable for them to request this government to take care of the weeds on crown lands which are under federal control. Of course those farmers know perfectly well that if the government carries out such a course they will have to pay their share of the cost of doing it, the expenditure will have to be met by a tax, but even so would it not be advisable for this government to take the necessary steps. To my personal knowledge this matter has been before the government for some considerable

The Address-Mr. Stewart (Humboldt)
time, and I would urge them to take the required steps before the problem becomes such a serious one that it can only be handled through the instrumentality of a severe tax. Therefore I urge the government to tackle this problem now and do their best to eradicate the weeds on crown lands adjacent to cultivated lands.
One other thing that personal endeavour is doing for many farmers, and they are finding it to be of great assistance to them, is specialization in some particular line or branch of their industry, and I want to quote just one incident that came to my attention in that regard. Not very long ago-to be precise less than two months ago-I was talking to two gentlemen and it was perhaps a coincidence that each of these gentlemen, engaged in farming in western Canada, has a brother sitting in this House. We were discussing the matter of the unprofitableness of farming at the present time. One of these men made the statement, and he is a farmer on a large scale, that when he had cleaned up he would have to dig into his capital, as he has had to do for two or three years, to square himself up, and yet he had had good results so far as yields were concerned. The other man farming in the same community with him made the statement-and he gave me some details later on which, I think, would adequately prove his statement-that the past year's crop was going to be the most profitable he had ever harvested in western Canada. The two men are farming within a very few miles of one another but the difference was this: The one man was farming-I was going to say wholly along wheat growing lines but that would not be correct, he does keep the average number of live stock, cattle and hogs on his farm; but the other man is a specialist in the growing of clover. It was just along the line of that specialization that he had received the big returns from his last year's crop, and I believe that farmers by specializing where the opportunity offers will obtain good returns.
Now I must hurry on to the next point and that is co-operative effort to better conditions. This is receiving very considerable attention in Canada at the present time, particularly wheat marketing in western Canada. I do not wish to say very much in regard to that, it is in an experimental stage so far, but the indications are that it will vindicate the test and that the results of wheat marketing by co-operative methods will indeed be proved within a year or two in this Dominion, just as other commodities of the farmer have been marketed successfully through co-operative methods. In the province of Saskatchewan in some instances we market our live stock through the initial stages co-operatively. In my own experience we organized a co-operative stock shipping association some ten or twelve years ago. In so far as hogs are concerned, the prices were not very high at that time, but our returns for hogs through shipping co-operatively increased about 33 1/3 per cent immediately over the price we had previously been receiving. As to cattle the returns were not so obvious but they were very satisfactory, and to this extent, that in the district where that stock shipping was organized, for two years after the system was inaugurated no drover shipped a car of stock from that point; the shipments of cattle and hogs were all made co-operatively.
I also wish to mention the co-operative marketing of dairy products. In the province of Saskatchewan we have found that to be a very great success indeed. Although a moment ago I drpw the attention of the minister to the need for further activity on his part I would, just at this stage, give him due credit for the part he took in encouraging that system of co-operation in the marketing of dairy products, particularly cream and butter. There can be further co-operation. It has already been proved that co-operation is, to some extent, successful in the purchasing of commodities that are used in large quantities such as binder-twine, building materials and fencing. I am not going to enter into that.
I simply mention it as one of the things that has been tried and proved successful as a relief for conditions such as now exist. Then further, co-operation in a community can sometimes be made very valuable and laboursaving can be effected by co-operative efforts, particularly in the matter of the threshing of our grain crop. I think that this is one thing that requires the attention of the farmers themselves, and that efforts should be made along that line.
I come now to the third point, and the one which I wish to stress most in this House, because here we have an opportunity of taking steps along the lines that I indicate; that is, legislative reforms. First of all, I have placed the need of the reduction of federal taxation by the practice of economy in administration. With that simple statement, I think I have lined myself up with the great majority of the members in this House, and I am going to add nothing further at this time. Following that I would suggest an adjustment of the burden of taxation, so that the burden will not fall so heavily on the consumer; and in
8	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Stewart (Humboldt)
conjunction with that the adoption of direct methods of taxation. I know that we have many of them at the present time. I favour the adoption of direct methods, so that it will be more clearly indicated who pays the taxes. If I may be pardoned again for diverging from the subject in hand, I cannot help reading an editorial comment from a journal-I suppose it is a very reputable journal-published in Montreal, called the Montreal Pharmaceutical Journal. It is the last issue which I received February, 1924. In this journal a very misleading statement is published, and I am going to offer it to members of this House as something that will not get us anywhere, and something that we should discourage. We should face the facts, and these are not facts-at least they are not all facts. Some of the premises are perhaps facts. This article says-
Again we reiterate the statement that we are in Canada improperly taxed; that the taxation and vanous schemes of levy in effect are not alone onerous but depressing and destructive of energy and enterprise.
I think I could agree with that.
All the revenue required can be derived from a properly constructed customs tariff.
I think hon. members to my right can go that far, but I cannot.
Taxation levied through that channel applies to alleach and everyone living in the country would become a contributor whereas to-day there is current to a certain extent a class taxation that is manifestly unfair.
But it does not specify.
The farmers escape altogether.
I draw the attention of hon. members to that statement.
Whereas they would be just as happy if they were contributing moderately under the effect of meeting figures for their daily requirements that would constitute this contribution and practically without their being aware of it.
The editor holds that up as an ideal system of taxation. I, Sir, condemn it as being the worst system of taxation we could possibly have, and the sooner we get away from it the better for all.
The third suggestion that I am making in the way of legislative reforms would be the removal of the tariff from the necessaries of life and from the implements of production, as a means of lowering the cost of living. I have already made certain comments along that line and will not further comment.
I have another thing which is not exactly legislation, but which would require legislation if it could be effected. I appeal to the government to keep before them the need 
for constant endeavour to secure free entry for our goods to our natural market, namely the market of the great republic to the south of us.
Then there should be a thorough investigation of transportation costs, with a view to legislation where necessary to reduce them to a possible minimun. So far as our railways are concerned, I do not suppose that, with our National Railway piling up a deficit year after year, we are likely to get much sympathy m our requests for reductions of rates, but it has already been intimated to the government, not only this session but in past sessions a? well, that a revaluation of the capitalization of our Canadian National Railways might place them in a much better situation. I am inclined to believe that it would be proper to proceed along that line. So far as controlling lake transportation is concerned, I would suggest that the government take whatever steps are necessary to prevent a fiasco such as we witnessed last year occurring in the future, and I cannot see any reason in the world why, with a merchant marine at their command, they cannot offer as much competition to those unruly lake carriers as the situation calls for. Speaking of the merchant marine, I think that they could, if they so desired, use it to some extent at least to help us control the ocean transportation costs on our export live stock at least.
There is another suggestion along this same line. I suggest that the grain trade requires even more careful regulation than it has received up to the present time. I would suggest that attention be given to the grading of our grain-that is our wheat-based on its milling values, rather than on the basis which . now used, and also that a further investi-; gation should be made as to the effect of Imixing in our terminal elevators on our ultimate market for grain. Then I would suggest, along a different line, that we should proceed with our investigation which was begun last year to try and find a system for providing long term and intermediate term credits. I am not going to enlarge upon it.
I would simply point it out. It is one of the things which I consider would render a considerable amount of relief to those suffering under adverse circumstances.
Lastly, I would suggest to the government that new or increased transportation facilities would to a certain extent relieve the difficulties that we suffer under at the present time. There are, Sir, three projects before this House at the present time for consideration; the St. Lawrence deep waterway project, the Pacific route for our grain and the Hudson Bay route.

The Address-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
At this particular time I do not intend to debate the relative value of those routes. I simply suggest to the government that they should investigate very thoroughly the possibilities of those routes, and, before I make any further statement, may I say that the Hudson Bay route cannot be properly investigated until the road is completed to the bay, and I think it is only a fair and just demand of all the agriculturists who are living in western Canada, and who are interested in that route, that the railway be completed to the bay. Then having placed that route on a fair footing with the other routes I think the government should investigate all of them and should develop those that show they would return an adequate interest on the investment made in them. I have made these suggestions, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that I might draw attention to some of the causes of and some of the remedies for the conditions under which agriculture suffers. I have already apologized to the House for the many figures I have imposed upon it. and I trust I will be forgiven for trespassing at such length upon the time of the House.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Address-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
upon, is a policy of protection, not only to the manufacturer but to the agriculturist.
And what do we ask in addition? We ask the government to stop what I would call "the mad dog" policy which it is pursuing at the present time. The newspapers of the country, the bankers and other personages urge upon them retrenchment. "Yes," the government said "we will retrench. We will begin with the Auditor General. We will retrench his salary from S6,000 to $15,000. We will place that official in charge of the rest of the retrenchments. We will place him in charge of putting out the little fish, of throwing out the little fellow, with a salary of $1,000 a year. This is the man who is to be thrown out and the man with an increase of $9,000 a year is to have charge of the work." Not only that but I understand an order has gone out to the deputy ministers to retrench, to cut 25 per cent off their estimates, to cut 25 per cent off here and there. It is, as I said before, a mad dog policy. The government are biting here and biting there; they have no order or system whatever in regard to their retrenchments.
We also ask the government to lessen the income tax. We do not say that the income tax should be abolished in its entirety, but we have gone so far in this method of taxation to-day that people are afraid to go any further in the direction of developing industry. They are afraid to put their money into any work that will give employment to others in this country. If we do nothing else we can surely lessen the income tax of those who are producing work, who are carrying out development in this country to some extent, and give them some relief so that the money now being taken from them will be placed back in industry and help to further develop the industrial life of the country.
We also say to the government:	Spend
less money on undesirable and inexcusable immigration policies. It is a sad state of affairs to-day that people are being brought out to Canada when there is no work for them. I am not speaking now of the harvesters who were induced to come to Canada, but a few weeks ago it was my experience to meet six of the finest Scottish lads I ever saw. They had been brought out to Canada by a notice in the paper saying that there was work to be found in this country. They had put up all the money they had to reach the Dominion only to find that conditions here were just about as bad as they were in the Old Country. It is possible that some of the people brought here have been provided with employment, but how

many of them have only swollen the ranks of the unemployed by coming to Canada.
Now, Sir, I have spoken of this administration as a wobbling government, a vacillating government. Many parts of Canada are awaiting an answer as to what the government intend to do in regard to certain issues. There is, for example, a demand for the deepening of the St. Lawrence, for the completion of the Welland canal, for the selection of a terminal for the Great Lakes development. If the present policy of the government continues there will be no necessity for them to act more speedily than they are now doing. There will be no industries to demand the electrical current which the province of Ontario expects to obtain from the St. Lawrence waterway development. There will be no need for any further increase of electrical power in the Welland canal district. In cities like Brantford industries will perhaps close, the wheels of the mills there will no longer be grinding and turning. Even now the outlook is by no means so rosy as the Speech from the Throne declares. But there is one thing we do expect, unless the government take so long to consider their policy that the people in their anger will rise and cast them out, and that is that some day they will give an answer to the various great questions which are being pressed upon them by the people of Canada.
On motion of Mr. Speakman the debate was adjourned. *
